Biographia documentata

Documented biography

by Gian Lodovico Masetti Zannini

At the request of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints and at the invitation of the Postulation of the Cause, Prof. Gian Lodovico Masetti Zannini has written the following documented biography of the Servant of God, which is now included here as an integral part of this Positio.

The author, Prof. Gian Lodovico Masetti Zannini,* well known at the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, where he has served as a Consultor since 1987, holds a diploma in language and literature from the University of Heidelberg and a degree in law from the University of Milan.

Though brief, the biography makes an excellent contribution to the Cause of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Besides examining all the documents made available to him by the Postulation, the professor personally consulted the Archive of the Generalate of the Daughters of Saint Anne, as well as the archives of Palermo, Florence and Rome and the Vatican Archives, and so was able to reconstruct on solid foundations and with complete fidelity the life of the Servant of God in her historical period and in the settings (the various communities of the North, the Center and Sicily) where she lived and carried out her mission.

Sincerely grateful to the Author for his work, the Petitioners also express their special thanks to the Most Rev. Father Eszer, Relator, for wishing to enrich the Positio with this biography.

The Postulation

After years of research and study on the virtuous life of our sister, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Prof. Count Gian Ludovico Masetti Zannini has completed, with intelligent and admirable dedication, the new Documented Biography requested by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints for the continuation of the inquiry into the Cause of Beatification and Canonization so dear to our hearts.

This careful work, historically precise thanks also to newly acquired documents, enriches and completes the two previous biographies, allowing us to piece together a mosaic of grace and virtue that reveals “today” too the possibility of fulfilling “God’s dream” for his creatures: holiness.

We therefore welcome this study with joyful gratitude, followed carefully step by step by the Postulation, in the earnest hope that it may edify us and all people of good will, for the greater glory of God and of his faithful Servant, Sister Anna del Salvatore.

It must be said at once that anyone who leafs through this biography expecting to find extraordinary events will certainly be disappointed, so simple and ordinary was her life.

Passing quickly among us, almost on tiptoe, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, born Marianna, left in every place touched by her mission a vivid reflection of her goodness, in those who enjoyed her friendship and in those who had the grace of having her beside them in times of illness and suffering.

To know this “Daughter of Saint Anne” a little more closely, however, we must go back to God’s overflowing love for his creatures and approach the mystery of his free choice of persons, to whom he entrusts the sublime project of reproducing authentically and radically the features of his Son Jesus, radiating above all mercy, goodness, gentleness and humility, especially towards the little ones and the poor.

Sister Anna del Salvatore certainly grasped within herself this gesture of infinite predilection and responded to it with constancy, tenacity and suffering, with readiness and acceptance of all that would gradually be revealed as God’s will for her.

Grace prevailed in her life at every moment. The Sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation, received at a very tender age, found in the little girl a setting already prepared to produce the effects they signify. The Christian formation she breathed in her family, with its particular emphasis on sacrifice, renunciation and mortification, would train her in a “taste” for the essential, not only in the ordinary things of daily life but also and above all in the things of the spirit.

And so Marianna, trained from childhood in a life of piety and devotion, would soon immerse her whole life, her heart and her love in Jesus in the Eucharist.

Although it is difficult to trace any extraordinary events that may have occurred during the hours and nights she spent in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, there is no doubt that Sister Anna del Salvatore, precisely through those mysterious, ineffable conversations with Jesus, found in the Master’s heart the center and foundation of her transformation and conformity to him, clothing herself with humility and obedience, gentleness and charity and all the other virtues that would later adorn her life in complete anonymity and in perfect heroism. Like the bride of the “Song of Songs”, she longed only for the Beloved, so that, utterly faithful to the inner impulse that drove her to seek him constantly, she came at a certain point to be almost assimilated, in a wonderful crescendo, to the light that had always enlightened and guided her. With Saint Augustine she could surely say: “With the eye of my soul, such as it was, I saw an unchangeable light above my inner gaze and above my mind. It was not the ordinary light visible to every eye. It would be too little to say that it was merely a stronger light than the ordinary, or one so intense that it penetrated all things. It was another light, very different from all the lights of creation. It was not above my mind as oil floats on water or as the sky stretches over the earth; it was a higher light. It was the light that made me” (from the Confessions of Saint Augustine).

On Sister Anna del Salvatore’s path to perfection one cannot overlook her relationship with the Foundress, Mother Rosa Gattorno, now Blessed: a relationship rooted in a close and unmistakable bond of maternal and filial love; in a frank, free and sincere rapport bordering on the incredible; in such mutual esteem, trust and self-giving that they seemed “kindred spirits”; and in a convergence and communion of thoughts and ideals springing from a single source and flowing towards a single goal: God in others.

Who Mother Rosa was for Sister Anna del Salvatore and what she meant to her can be understood from the way she obeyed. There is no doubt that faith and humility led her to see in the Foundress the channel of Grace through which God’s will reached her unaltered; so she became her faithful disciple, the one most identified with her spirit.

For Sister Anna del Salvatore the Mother was the authentic, luminous reflection of the Face of Christ Crucified, by whose light she let herself be penetrated and drawn in order to renew her strength and fidelity in following him, “obedient unto death, even death on a cross!”

The Crucified, the Eucharist, following in the footsteps of the Mother, a living charism, and the world of suffering and pain: these were the ever-open books in which Sister Anna del Salvatore immersed herself, letting herself be formed ever more deeply on the path of perfect charity until she reached, as in fact she did, the offering of herself, out of love alone.

Such an example of life challenges our times, because it questions our subtle desires for independence and self-importance, disguised beneath various theories of personal fulfilment and self-assertion; and because, whereas Sister Anna del Salvatore, open and docile to the action of the Spirit, went straight to the source of Wisdom, we sometimes seek it in the labyrinth of human knowledge, often finding in our hands many novelties that “make the news” but struggle to build or give stability to new paths of life and hope, “stirring the people of our time... who thirst for absolute values” (VC 93f).

For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and thwart the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Cor 1:19). And Jesus said: “I bless you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little ones” (Mt 11:25).

Through her experience of service and selflessness, of closeness to the weakest, of simplicity, humility and awareness of human frailty, Sister Anna del Salvatore sowed peace, love and fraternity everywhere and bore witness to “the fatherly face of God and the motherly face of the Church”, staking “her own life so that others may have life and hope” (VC 105b).

Among the stars that form a crown around Saint Anne in heaven, the brightness of the star of this daughter of hers certainly stands out: completely emptied of self and given over to the love of Jesus, she lost herself in him and became as he wished: little, “gentle and humble of heart”.

Therefore she could make her name, written in heaven from all eternity, shine with intense light.

Rome, 14 October 2004.

Sister A. Maria Luisa Prandina

Superior General

“Be good and obedient.” These were the last words of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi. She spoke them on 7 June 1885 at 11 p.m., before returning to the Lord, whom she had loved intensely and tenderly throughout the 43 years of her life.

Professor Masetti Zannini’s detailed account of this life can be read in one sitting. It portrays a life that, at an ever-quickening pace, became a model of docility to the Lord and to the religious Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which she entered as a novice at 26, in November 1868. She lived with ardor the momentous early years, marked by the motherly care of Mother Rosa Gattorno, who personally followed the development of the Congregation; and she followed her directives with filial docility.

The impression that takes root in mind and heart, page after page, is that of a saint of obedience. The unreserved and transparent openness and trust with which she turned to the Mother are moving and exemplary.

Her union with God during her 17 years in the Congregation passed through her docile and filial relationship with Mother Rosa.

It is hard to draw the line between the immense inventiveness of her charity and her docility to the Mother. Her life is a song of thanksgiving for two alternating voices, constantly addressed to the same invisible Master.

For Masetti this seems to be the chief feature of the lives of these two women whose hearts beat as one in docility to the Lord, loved and served in the poor, the sick, people in need and in the education of young women.

The events of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s life were anything but simple and straightforward. The tasks the Mother entrusted to her were always extremely delicate. The trials of the foundation in Florence, and those of founding the communities first in Palermo and then throughout Sicily after she became Provincial in 1884, were a source of suffering lived in adoration and penance. All this shows how hard it is to do good well for love of the Good Father, and how much sacrifice and prayer nourish and enliven the attraction that she and her Sisters had for everyone who, through them, experienced the tenderness of God’s love. Their lives were not simply inspired by the spirituality of the time, but sprang from the tenderness of a genuine femininity that finds joy in conforming to the path walked by Christ, described in moving terms by Saint Peter in his First Letter (2:21-25).

Anyone who knows the history of the beginnings of the family of the Daughters of Saint Anne notices that their most significant feature is a most tender imitation of the sufferings of Christ, the inexhaustible source of gentleness and transparency in every life. Of all of them it may be said: by his wounds we have been healed; we were straying like sheep, but now we have returned to the shepherd and guardian of our souls (ibid. 25).

Sister Anna del Salvatore’s tireless activity was not an expression of mere activism or a craving for omnipotence; it drew its inspiration from the Sitio (“I thirst”) of Jesus’ Cross, which burned in her heart and fed her kindness towards the poorest. It was also inspired by the example of Blessed Rosa Gattorno, which was reflected by osmosis in her soul and from her spread to all who approached her or felt her attraction.

She too had to keep watch, firm in faith, to resist the snares of the “divider”, the devil, who prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour (ibid. 5:9).

As often happens in God’s works, the greatest resistance she faced came from those who should have most supported her fervor.

By her example Sister Anna del Salvatore shows that the strength of martyrdom does not come from not suffering violence but from not allowing it to weaken one’s fidelity to the One who left us an example so that we might follow in his steps (ibid. 2:21).

Her obedience to the Mother, which led her constantly to seek advice and to submit even the simplest initiatives for approval, did not stifle the source of her creativity and resourcefulness, which on the one hand, through her intense activity, sorely tested her strength and on the other renewed her vigor. One day in May 1885, a month before her death, when her health was already undermined by illness and a high fever kept her in bed, she received a telegram from the Mother ordering her to go from Palermo to Trapani on an urgent matter concerning the recently opened community; ignoring the fever, she left at once. She carried out her task and returned to Palermo exhausted.

Some episodes of her life may give the impression of excessive attachment to solving the many problems of the communities for which she was responsible. In fact this is the realizm of holiness, which has nothing to do with an obsession with success. She took care of and was concerned for the people who were to devote their lives to others; she wanted them free from the worries that undermine daily survival and which, without a minimum of peace and serenity, in the long run dry up the source of self-giving.

To present this most delicate figure of a woman and a religious to the contemporary world is to profess faith in God’s mercy and to invite people to open the eyes of the Spirit and see around us the presence of so many Sisters Anna del Salvatore who follow in her footsteps and find peace of mind and heart in contemplating the Lord through total and generous self-giving for the good of others. We would all like to meet someone like her on our path of sorrow, so as to recognize that the grace of the Spirit works in simple and ordinary people too. If we were more docile to the action of the Spirit we would experience the same joy and would promote God’s glory through active and sincere friendship with those who are called to live “in”, “with” and “through” us as children of the Father of Mercy.

Sister Anna del Salvatore’s personality speaks not only to the Daughters of Saint Anne, reminding them of the vigor of their beginnings and of the hard day that began at 4.30 a.m. with morning prayers and ended so late that there was no time left to gather together. It speaks to all women and men who, in this age of globalized economic interests, go on believing in mercy amid the immense sufferings of a world in which the rich grow ever more ruthless in pursuing their interests and the poor, especially the elderly and the suffering, are increasingly condemned to a loneliness that the Lord consoles but that the visible presence of generous people helps to make more bearable.

Sister Anna del Salvatore’s experience is confirmed by all those who, having given everything, wonder how it was possible and where the strength came from that keeps them going and is continually renewed, just like mercy, which grows when it is received and shared.

Bari, 27 October 2004.

Fr. Dalmazio Mongillo, O.P.

1. - It was the year of grace 1842 when, on 22 February, Marianna Orsi was born, the first child of Angelo and Margherita Mussi, both from Albareto and smallholders of a house and land in that village of the Duchy of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla, formerly ruled by the Farnese and the Bourbons but at that time governed by Archduchess Marie Louise of Habsburg, daughter of Emperor Francis I and widow of Napoleon Bonaparte. On her death six years later the Bourbons would return. Charles Louis, formerly King of Etruria and until then Duke of Lucca, later abdicated in favor of his son Charles III, the penultimate ruler of the Farnese duchies.

We have various details about the birthplace and environment in which the future Sister Anna del Salvatore was brought up, collected by the parish priest, a contemporary of the Servant of God, who describes them as follows:

“Albareto, formerly also Albereto, a large village in the valley of the Gotra on the right bank of that stream, chief town of the commune of the same name, lies 7 km south-south-west of Borgotaro […]. The boundaries of its territory are, I would almost say, set by nature […]. The territory of Albareto is crossed by two streams, one called the Rio Barbigarezza and the other the Ruffinà, or rather Rio finale. The latter divides the village into two distinct parts, so that the part on its right is called Albareto and that on its left Mamponeto. There are also various other channels, such as the Pighenzola, Lavacchio, Rossetta, etc.

The houses are scattered in various family groups forming different hamlets […]. In general the dwellings are rustic, too cramped for the necessities of life, badly built without any plan, and leave much to be desired also from the point of view of hygiene.”

In the early years of the twentieth century Albareto had 244 houses, 167 families and a total of 926 souls; while the climate could be called good for the purity and healthiness of the air, the winters were very harsh and the north winds kept the heavy snowfalls on the ground well into spring, thus delaying the growth of vegetation and work in the fields. Moreover, when heavy rain fell, the many winding paths linking the scattered houses, which often served as drains for the fields, turned into torrents.1

These and other details, provided by a zealous pastor of souls and by long experience, make it clear how hard and difficult life was in those places, especially for those who earned their daily bread working the land.

Albareto today (brief notes)

2. - Albareto is today the chief town of the commune of the same name in the province of Parma, in the upper Taro valley, between 421 and 1,639 m above sea level, near Borgo Val di Taro, the main town of the valley (now with about 5,000 inhabitants).

The commune of Albareto covers almost 104 km² and lies mostly on the right bank of the Taro, in the valley of its tributary the Gotra, which flows down from Mount Gottero; this mountain marks the watershed between the valleys of the Taro, of the Vara in the province of La Spezia (Liguria), and of the Magra, which flows through the Lunigiana (in the Tuscan province of Massa Carrara).

At the end of 2000 its population numbered 2,164; it had aged considerably (31.1% elderly) and fallen sharply (by 48%) compared with the 1951 census, when it numbered 4,162 (and the elderly made up only 9.9%).

The population’s economic situation is modest; in 1995 taxable income per inhabitant was over a third below the provincial average.3

In the past the commune lacked an urban center larger than the other settlements in its territory.

In the last published census, for 1991, ISTAT classifies as “inhabited centers” the localities of Albareto (413 inhabitants), Boschetto (52), Gotra (147) and Montegroppo (85); it then lists 21 “inhabited nuclei”, including Buzzò (37 inhabitants), Cacciarasca (20), Campi (43), Codogno (26), Folta (38), Pieve di Campi (11) and San Quirico (48).4

If we look at how the population of the hamlet of Albareto, seat of the Town Hall and the parish church, was distributed even just fifty years ago, in 1951, we find that the village itself had only about a hundred inhabitants; the rest were divided among some fifteen settlements and, to a large extent, among “scattered houses”:

This was even truer in the nineteenth century, so much so that Don Tommaso Grilli, parish priest there from 1859 to 1923, noted that “The position of the parish church is very inconvenient for almost the whole population, being built on the bank of the Gotra at the boundary; and it was a mistake not to rebuild it recently at Costello, a central place convenient for all its hamlets.”5

As regards church boundaries, the commune of Albareto today includes the parishes of Cacciarasca (82 inhabitants), Campi (200), Codogno (100), Folta and Tombeto (together 66), Groppo (50) and Boschetto (170), Montegroppo (120), Pieve di Campi (200) and San Quirico (123) in the diocese of Piacenza,6 and the parishes of Albareto, Buzzò and Gotra in the diocese of Massa Carrara-Pontremoli.

To understand how these localities, though in the Province of Parma, depend on the Diocese of Piacenza (to which all the localities of the middle and upper Ceno and Taro valleys belong)7 and on the Diocese of Pontremoli,8 we must retrace the complex history of these border lands, which we shall now do very briefly.

A land of borders and passes

3. - The Ligurians are the first historically known people to have lived in the upper Taro valley; they were defeated and subjugated by the Romans in 187 BC after decades of bitter fighting.9

The Romans colonized the territory, organizing its agriculture and incorporating it into the Municipium of Veleia;10 scholars believe that from antiquity and for many centuries there was an important route between Veleia and Luni, though they debate its possible course or courses; this route necessarily crossed the upper Taro valley, using the Bratello and/or Cento Croci passes, east and west of Mount Gottero respectively.11

When Rome’s power declined, peoples from outside the empire invaded Italy; an authoritative scholar of the place names of the Ceno and Taro valleys believes that the names Gotra and Gottero bear witness to the presence of the Goths in these mountains.12

The Goths were successfully opposed by the Byzantines, who fortified their positions in the Taro valley too; the name of Campi, a hamlet of Albareto, may derive from their kàstron Kàmpsas.13

Byzantine rule did not last long; soon a new people arrived who would leave a lasting, in a sense “definitive”, mark on these lands through their presence and culture: the Lombards.

Their king Authari conquered the Taro valley at the end of the sixth century, though it was Liutprand, in the mid-eighth century, who completed the conquest of the Apennines; for a long time the watershed between the Po valley and Liguria was a border zone and perhaps one of disputes and friction.

The Lombard kings encouraged the founding of powerful monasteries that would accumulate vast estates, partly through royal donations; two should be mentioned for their influence on this area: San Colombano of Bobbio, founded by Agilulf in 614, and the Monastery of Brugnato, probably founded by the monks of Bobbio.14

The Gotra area became the property of the Monastery of Brugnato,15 which established a monastic cella or priory there;16 the Albareto area belonged to the Monastery of San Caprasio of Aulla, while in the tenth century a curtis at Groppo is recorded as belonging to the Monastery of Bobbio.17

In 1219 Venacio, abbot of the monastery of Aulla, sold to the Commune of Piacenza all the property the monastery owned in Albareto.18

According to Don Tommaso Grilli,

“in 1133 [...] when the ancient abbey of Brugnato was raised to episcopal rank, the villages of Gotra, Buzzò and Zeri19 were joined to this new diocese; Albareto always remained under the bishopric of Luni.20 At that time it cannot be said to have been joined to any other parish of its diocese, for it was surrounded on all sides by the territory of other Dioceses: that of Brugnato through Gotra, Buzzò and Zeri, and that of Piacenza through Tombeto, San Quirico and Campi; and Albareto remained in this border situation until 1854,” when it was joined to the Diocese of Pontremoli (formally established almost seventy years earlier).21

“It is also certain,” Don Tommaso continues, “that in 1219 Albareto was a parish, since the abbot Nicolli of Piacenza, in his work already cited, vol. 2, p. 1902,22 records a deed of that year by a certain notary Guglielmo Decelolis concerning the investiture of a certain Giovanni Savino, ante Ecclesiam de Albareto, with some feudal properties at Tiedoli, apud Castrum Tegeti.”23

“Towards the middle of the present century [i.e. the nineteenth], since, according to some, the government of Parma did not wish to have in its duchy parishes subject to the bishops of the Subalpine Kingdom, where the air of Italian nationalism was blowing, Albareto, Baselica and Valdena,24 together with Gotra and Buzzò, the latter two belonging to the Bishopric of Brugnato, were joined to the Diocese of Pontremoli by a Consistorial Decree dated Rome, 9 August 1854.

Before 1797 this parish was subject to the vicariate forane of Pontremoli, then to that of Baselica di Pontolo, and from 1856 onwards to that of Gotra.”25

We have briefly outlined the history of church jurisdiction over the territory of the commune of Albareto up to 150 years ago, that is, the time when Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi was born and lived there, when it was divided among three Dioceses, and since then, to this day, between two.

We should now mention civil jurisdiction, but that would be too long a subject and essentially outside the purpose of these notes. Suffice it to say that around the year 1000 the upper Taro valley was strongly influenced by the Malaspina and the Counts of Lavagna on the one hand and by the Commune of Piacenza on the other; the latter prevailed in the twelfth century. In the following centuries the little world of the Taro valley was divided between the Ghibelline state of the Landi (comprising Compiano, Bedonia and Tornolo) and the territory of Borgotaro, which included Albareto, for a long time a Guelph lordship of the Fieschi, a branch of the Counts of Lavagna who were for centuries hostile to the Landi; from the mid-sixteenth century the Fieschi were replaced by the Farnese, who had become Dukes of Parma and Piacenza.

Only in 1682, on the death of the last of the Landi, Polissena, were the Farnese able to buy the Landi State from the Doria, her heirs, and reunite the jurisdiction of the upper Taro valley by incorporating it into the Duchy.

In the eighteenth century and up to the Napoleonic era the Farnese were succeeded by the Bourbons; after Ferdinand’s death in 1802 the French administration took over; after the Corsican’s defeat the Duchy of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla was given to his far from inconsolable wife (and, above all, daughter of the Emperor of Austria), Marie Louise of Habsburg, who ruled it until her death at the end of 1847, when Sister Anna was a child.26

Then the Bourbons returned for a few years, until the unification of Italy.

Albareto in the nineteenth century: population and civic organization

4. - During the French administration Albareto ceased to be part of the Community of Borgotaro and was joined to the new Commune of Valdena, created in 1805, which comprised the right bank of the Taro from the Cogena to the Lubiana; “this commune,” adds Don Grilli, “under that French administrative division, belonged to the Canton and District of Borgotaro, the prefecture of Chiavari and the department of the Apennines”; the first maire (mayor) was Luigi Barbieri of Valdena.

When French rule ended in 1814, a decree of the Duchy of Parma made Albareto the chief town of the commune of the same name, with a territory of just over 100 km² comprising the comunelli (small communities) of Albareto, Buzzò, Cacciarasca, Campi, Codogno, Folta, Gotra, Groppo, Monte Groppo, Pieve di Campi, San Quirico and Tombeto.

The first podestà (mayor) was Stefano Capitelli of Pieve di Campi, followed by:

- Quirico Maestri of San Quirico;

- Francesco Mussi of Albareto;

- Luigi Balduini of San Quirico;

- Luigi Ferrari of Cacciarasca;

- Domenico Balduini, son of Giovanni, of San Quirico;

- Lorenzo Mussi of Albareto;

- Federico Gennari of Campi;

- Domenico Bosi of Albareto;

- Cav. Domenico Balduini of San Quirico.

The last of these was in office in 1893, the year Don Grilli’s Manipolo di Cognizioni... was published; some of the mayors, the Author notes, held office more than once.27

As we have said, the settlement pattern of Albareto in the nineteenth century was rather unusual; it lacked a “center”, consisting rather of a collection of farmhouses scattered or grouped in small clusters; Molossi describes it as “a hamlet of the Duchy of Parma with about 24 hearths and 120 inhabitants”, adding that “the territory of the village proper numbers 637 inhabitants”.28

Cenni Storici di Albareto reproduces a very interesting “List of the entire population of the parish of St Mary of Albareto made on 31 July 1821 by the parish priest Don Lodovico Bosi”, taken from the parish “Status animarum”; it lists the localities and the resident families, about 130, giving for each the name and surname of the head of the family and some members, and almost always the nickname, a necessary device for identifying people where so many shared the same name.

At the end of the list he adds the following note:

“The above Individuals of the Parish of Albareto, as far as I the undersigned know, are all of Christian principles; none meddles in the political affairs of Government, and their chief occupation is tilling the land, except the infirm and the Poor, and Children and Clergy. / Lodovico Bosi - Rector.”

The list begins with the locality of Le Moje, where the Orsi29 “Anierèn” lived, the family to which Sister Anna del Salvatore belonged; Le Moje lies on the floor of the Gotra valley at about 485 m above sea level, in an area that is more hilly than mountainous (unlike the whole upper part of the commune); it is situated, as Boccia wrote, “a mile below the Church of Albareto”.30

Don Grilli notes that Anna [Sister A. del Salvatore] “from Le Moie, together with her devout mother, ‘heard Holy Mass daily’”.31

Examination of the Land Register (volume 2) and maps (Section G, sheet 1, canton 5) of the former Cadastre of the Commune of Albareto, surveyed in 1824, shows that at Le Moje, among the properties belonging to the Orsi, was that of Fr. Stefano Orsi and his brother, living in Albareto, which included, among others, plots 476 (farmhouse with courtyard), 472 (farmhouse) and 438 (single-wheel grain mill).

Sister Orsi’s birthplace, now owned by Signora Bice Borella, can still be identified and corresponds (subject to more careful verification) to plot 476 of the old Cadastre.

The hamlet of Le Moie lies to the left of the provincial road to Albareto, just after crossing the Barbigareccio stream; all the buildings except one, which retains the features of the poor local architecture of the past, have been profoundly altered in recent decades.

Before concluding, it is worth pausing to consider what was meant at that time by a “mill” or a “farmhouse”.

Suffice it to note that the area of the five plots of the mills at Le Moie ranged from 20 to 35 square meters; they were thus small buildings with thick stone walls and a single room barely large enough for the millstone and hopper (some examples of such mills, though no longer working, can still be found in the upper Taro valley).

As for the houses, it is enough to read these few lines by Don Grilli:

“In winter the families gather round the fire in the middle of the kitchen, which is all blackened and crusted with soot, on long wooden benches with high backs that shield them from the cold draughts outside and let them enjoy the healthy warmth of the flame, and many lie down on them after supper and sleep long and soundly. In some kitchens great fires are made with whole tree trunks, so that it is very warm, since above them is the sooty rack where the chestnuts are still dried; but usually there is also a great deal of smoke, which often brings tears to the eyes. Recently many families have begun using cast-iron stoves32 to avoid not only the cold but also the smoke.”33

Don Antonio Emmanueli wrote at about the same time:

“So many are the innovations introduced in the last fifty years [in the customs of our villages] that, if I did not point out this great change of scene, the reader might be badly mistaken in supposing that the old customs still survive, whereas today they are very different. The houses are no longer the same: neither glass nor chimneys were used, but simply cloth over the windows34 and open hearths in the middle of the kitchens with a slatted platform above to dry chestnuts. In this regard I have heard from an eyewitness that Fallot Beaumont, Bishop of Piacenza, visiting one of our chief villages in 1808, accused a priest of luxury because the windows of his house had glass in them; today, by contrast, there is no hovel without glazed windows and kitchens with stoves or chimneys.”35

Agriculture, “Comunalie” and other economic activities

5. - L. Molossi notes that the territory of Albareto

“produces wheat, pulses, chestnuts, excellent marrons, mushrooms in quantity, which are pickled in brine and sell well. Some broad beans, wine and maize are also grown [...].

The snow that lingers on the Apennines well into spring and falls very early in autumn greatly hinders the ripening of crops.

The woods are mostly of chestnut and beech, but little profit is drawn from the latter, since the inhabitants neglect the beechnuts36 and cannot transport the timber because of the bad roads.

Add to this the thefts and damage caused by the neighbors to the south [...].

Besides farming, the inhabitants raise oxen, sheep and goats. The cattle are a small breed, as are generally all those of the high mountains; moreover, the lack of or difficulty in trading livestock in those parts (once a flourishing trade) means that owners take little interest in it.

The waters of some of these streams [the Gotra and its tributaries] and of a few brooks keep 24 mills turning continuously, and another 20 work only for part of the year. All but 6 have a single wheel [...].

Others make baskets, tubs, small beech barrels and a great many oars, which they take to sell on the Genoese Riviera, and other goods that are then sold at nearby markets [...]. In the small community of Gotra a livestock fair is held on 26 July, attended by many people from the neighboring districts.”37

Don T. Grilli, writing sixty years after Molossi, notes that

“almost all the families own property38 and work the land. Since property is very fragmented and divided, cultivation is intensive and careful, and in the last few years it has made more progress than in the past [...]. In former times the poorer families lived in summer up in the chestnut woods, where they built dry-stone huts or huts walled with earth [...]. From time immemorial many families here used to take in large herds of goats from the Genoa region to graze from May to the end of October, undertaking to give their owners a set quantity of cheese.”39

He adds, with the optimism suggested by the frugality of the time, that

“their diet is simple and healthy, consisting of a daily flatbread of maize or chestnut flour (patona) baked under the testo (a domed lid), or polenta in the morning, and in the evening a soup of wheat noodles. With this they eat potatoes and beans. They eat fruit, fresh chestnuts40 cooked in various ways, and boiled dried chestnuts. Lard, cheese, ricotta, eggs and milk are used for flavoring, and little oil.”41

He cannot, however, help observing that

“the produce of farming and livestock has never been enough to meet the needs of a large part of the local population; so many have always taken up other crafts and trades.”42

Don Grilli then gives us a detailed list of the local “industries”:

“One local industry is gathering mushrooms, which grow here in quantity both in summer and in autumn”; once dried, “they sell them mostly to the merchants of Tarsogno, who take [them] to Genoa.”

“The cooper’s craft is ancient and practized by many, and they are very skilled at making vats, casks, barrels and buckets, which are highly praised and sold at the markets of Borgotaro, Varese Ligure, Pontremoli, Bardi and Bedonia.43

[...] There are still skilled craftsmen in this line [blacksmiths] to make or repair farm tools and other iron and steel goods [...]. Several families have looms and good weavers for making linen, half-wool and the homespun cloth called peluzzo, so that many people from the surrounding villages too bring them their yarn to be woven.

On the Lecora stream two fulling mills have been working since time immemorial. In the past people came even from distant places to have their woollen cloth fulled there.

Some people work as millers, since there are eight mills with several pairs of stones on the waters of Albareto. Some, however, cannot grind in summer for lack of water power, etc.

Recently basket-making too has been introduced here, and many men and women are very skilled at weaving willow withies into hampers, baskets and panniers, which they take to sell in the market squares of Varese Ligure and Pontremoli.44

There is no lack of fairly skilled shoemakers, tailors and seamstresses with sewing machines, which were introduced here after 1870.

There are innkeepers, grocers and sellers of state-monopoly goods.

In winter the women generally spin and knit, making things such as woollen gaiters, which they then sell, and other goods for their own families.

There are good masons who almost always have work repairing or building houses; they also do building carpentry, such as floors, shutters, doors and scaffolding, and go to work in other places too.

Some make half-moon-shaped cradles for babies out of thin beech boards, brightly painted and comfortable, which are sold in this district and beyond.”45

A feature of the upper Taro valley, and of the commune of Albareto in particular, is the survival of vast collective properties, especially large forests along the ridges.46

The Comunalia (common land) of Albareto covers 874 hectares47 and in the nineteenth century included “besides four plots of chestnut woods, the whole beech zone between the Tarodine and the Lecora”.48

Of course other income could come from time to time from the beech woods: thus in 1894 “the Comunalia of Albareto sold the beech wood above the Miravesco and Muradura channels to a Pontremoli firm, ‘Pinotti & C.’, for the sum of 45,000 lire” (equivalent today, using ISTAT revaluation coefficients for the lira, to over 285 million lire).49 The Comunalie still play a significant role in local life.

Trade and smuggling

6. - A land of borders and passes, Albareto too was, as we saw in the previous section, a land of trade and, until the unification of Italy, of smuggling.

Don Tommaso Grilli writes:

“Many of the local people go now to the Pontremoli area, now towards Sestri Levante, to buy oil, which they carry in skins on their own shoulders to sell in various villages of this District of Borgotaro; to get a better price they often go down into the lower hills. These oil-sellers then come back from those places laden with poultry, and sometimes they also bring turkeys, which they go and sell in the Genoa area.

Others trade in cattle and, mainly in summer, usually go to the Sarzana area, where a fine breed of bullocks is raised [...] [which] they sell at the large fairs and markets held in the Taro valley.

In former times, when the Grand Duchy of Tuscany bordered this territory across the Apennines, the trade of these villages was tied to Pontremoli, and smuggling was a real industry because of the difference in prices.

Salt cost 15 centesimi a kilogram in Pontremoli and twice as much in the Parma states, and the same was true of other goods.

So a great many people went to Pontremoli to buy salt, tobacco, gunpowder for hunting and various other goods, which they then sold at a profit in these villages of the Duchy of Parma.

Although they were very shrewd in their smuggling, using stratagems and taking little-known mountain paths, sometimes they fell into the hands of the customs guards and were taken to the prisons of Borgotaro.

Nevertheless some were fearless in this activity and sometimes banded together in large numbers, ready even to resist the authorities if opposed. And it is known that the guards, seeing the considerable number of smugglers, not infrequently thought it prudent to withdraw unseen so as not to risk a fight.”50

Traders, porters, muleteers, smugglers: these figures overlapped, and indeed were the same or different people depending on circumstances.51

Smuggling in the upper Taro valley lasted for centuries and was widespread: originally a way of avoiding the numerous and sometimes exorbitant tolls that goods had to pay not only in passing from one State to another but also from one Jurisdiction to another within the same State, or at bridges and fords, sometimes amounting to more than the value of the goods,52 over time, as trade increased, it increasingly became an organized traffic for moving goods clandestinely from Liguria towards the Duchy of Parma, Lombardy and Switzerland.53

Don Tommaso Grilli recalls, however, that the smugglers’ toil sometimes ended in tragedy:

“I must point out here, however, that a certain Giovanni Gallinari, son of the late Sabadino, from Tombeto, known as Carletto, was one of these daring men and very swaggering. Armed with a rifle, he was coming from Pontremoli laden with salt together with some others, and as he came down the mountain of Albareto, just after crossing the channel called Miravesco, the guards, seeing him armed and doubting his intentions, one of them fired at him; he rolled down below the road and died almost at once. The guards’ punishment,” Don Tommaso bitterly comments, “as far as is known, was a transfer to another Customs post.”54

Less dramatic was the outcome of the story of Domenico Bosi of Albareto, which deserves mention, partly because of the man’s unusual character.

Born in 1810, he had three paternal uncles who were priests, from whom he acquired some education; at 27 he was appointed mayor of Albareto; he married and had 22 children, 14 of whom survived infancy, and three of these became priests.

Physically imposing and enterprising, he too engaged in smuggling; so it happened that on 28 April 1848 (a very turbulent time in the Taro valley too, as we shall see) he quarrelled with the “préposés” (customs guards) and, backed by the “servants” who followed him, got the better of them and disarmed them.

Reported to the ducal authorities, he was pursued by dragoons, who captured him and took him to Parma; according to his own written account, however, he was acquitted, and he again served as mayor of Albareto between 1867 and 1869.55

The unification of Italy and the building of the railways put an end to this exhausting and risky form of struggle for survival among the mountain people, while accentuating another, already widespread phenomenon, emigration, on which we must dwell briefly.

Emigration

7. - Emigration too has a long history in the Taro valley; by a grida (proclamation) of 7 July 1596 Federico Landi, Principe de Valle Taro, ordered the registration of all land abandoned by owners who “se ne vanno in altre parti, lasciando derelitti i luoghi [...] con grand(issi)mo pregiud(iti)o dell’Ill(ustrissi)ma Sua Cam(er)a” (go off elsewhere, leaving their places derelict, to the very great detriment of His Most Illustrious Treasury):56 emigration from these lands was already well under way!

Mgr Ponzini places in the seventeenth century the episode recounted by Don Emmanueli, who, after recalling that at Groppo di Albareto

“there is a chapel of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, fully adorned, with a very beautiful marble statue”, relates that “all [this was done] through the efforts of a poor serving girl from here who, having gone to Genoa to work as a servant, throughout her life left most of her wages with her devout mistress for this pious purpose, and after her death her mistress faithfully carried out the pious intention of her lamented servant.”57

Molossi writes briefly of the commune of Albareto that “many go for a good part of the year to work beyond the Po or in the Maremma, since the total of present produce is not enough to support the whole population”.58

The imbalance between natural resources and population is stressed by Rufino Mussi in his report on the District of Borgotaro, written for the Agrarian Inquiry, known as the Jacini Inquiry, launched around 1880:

“This normal shortfall in meeting the needs of human sustenance is the scourge that most afflicts our farming class (...) Hence emigration, to send back from abroad what is needed to make up this deficit in the peasant families, which are thus deprived of their ablest and best workers.”59

He returns to the subject several times; thus, deploring the intolerable burden of taxes,60 he notes that

“our agriculture would not survive the crushing taxes if it had not extended cultivated land at the expense of waste ground (...) and if it were not reinvigorated by money from emigration”;61

for Albareto he specifies that

“there is emigration, generally not of people given to trade or other occupations not their own, but of workers who periodically, especially in winter, go as laborers to Marseilles or spread out across Provence to work in the olive-oil trade. There are also those who go to Paris or London, a few to trade, most as workers, and they always come back with some savings. It is noticeable that small landowners too take part in this emigration. Many farmers see its growth as a bad omen for the future of local production.”62

Don Tommaso Grilli, on the other hand, devotes a page to emigration that leans towards optimism:

“Finally, one main branch of industry in this village,” he writes, “is emigration. In times past the neediest went down in winter to the low plains of the Po to work at cleaning hemp, and many in May and June went to Lombardy to work in silkworm rearing; but these were meagre trades. Towards the middle of this century emigration began to turn towards France and England, and it has grown steadily year by year because travel has become easier since the railways were built.63

A great many young men and women, and many whole families, go to these countries; and not only those forced by need, but also many well-off landowners go there hoping to save and improve their situation, encouraged by the good fortune of those who went before them.

In London they make and sell ice cream from spring to autumn, always with a fair profit, and a larger one when the weather there is very hot.

In Paris and Marseilles they seek work as laborers in various factories and gasworks and, especially in the past, in street cleaning.

The workers are well paid and send money to their families, and bring back even more when they return, as long as they do not get caught up in the habits of those cities, for then all possibility of saving ends.

It should be noted that emigration to those places is now declining for various reasons, and in the last few years it has begun towards the United States of America. Husbands and wives, young people and whole families go there, and this emigration is growing year by year.”64

Don Antonio Emmanueli’s reading of emigration is much more worried; writing around 1885, he deplores the

“wretched craze that has seized our people of the Taro valley to leave their homeland and wander the world in search of fortune, not only on this side but also beyond the Atlantic. It is a sight to weep at,” he adds, “to see whole families, women, children and even babes in arms crossing the Ocean [...]. In the poorer villages,” he observes, “there were some instances of emigration in the past too, but in our day the abuse has gone beyond all bounds.”

He notes precisely:

“a small village in our district which in the 1871 census numbered 143 individuals now has no more than 78; all the others have flown, some to France, some to Germany, some to the Argentine Republic and more than 50 to the United States of America.”

“Almost all the other villages of our valley,” he concludes disconsolately, “are in much the same situation.”65

In reality the vast and prolonged emigration beyond the Alps from the Taro valley and neighboring valleys was marked by many, often indescribable, sacrifices and countless dramatic events.

Many never returned; Cenni Storici di Albareto relates that

“around 1830 a certain Penighetti (Stoccu) went from London to New York, the first person from Albareto to do so [...]; [he] traveled thousands of miles into the interior of the United States in search of his wife and son, who had joined the so-called pioneers in the conquest of the West. After ten years of fruitless searching, the poor man set off for home.”66

Don Tommaso Grilli notes that on 24 June 1898 “the French ship ‘Bourgogne’ sank; 500 emigrants bound for New York perished, among them three parishioners: Francesco Zecca, son of the late Domenico, his sister and his wife Clementina Bosi of the Lazzotti family”; heart-rending details of their end have been handed down.67

Many suffered poverty and inhuman exploitation.

“In our parts,” we read in Cenni Storici di Albareto, “there appeared from time to time a character known as the ‘One-eyed man of Grezzo’ (because he had lost an eye), who hired young people and led them across France to London. The journey took some forty days, measured not by the calendar but by the stick with which he provided the young emigrants. The stick kept its bark except at the bottom, which was peeled for about a ‘sëmèssu’, just under 20 cm. This ‘contractor’ told the youngsters, little more than boys: ‘When the part without bark has worn away completely, it means we have arrived.’”68

“Work abroad,” observes Don Tommaso Grilli, “has thus almost done away with the once widespread begging,69 and since many wish to turn the fruit of their labors into land, property has reached a much higher value than in the past.”70

“But,” Don Tommaso then observes, speaking of his parishioners’ customs, “now the periodic return of the emigrants [...] is bringing many innovations in dress and in local civil and domestic customs, so that greater cleanliness can already be seen in various respects.

And here it should be pointed out that while emigration has a favorable influence intellectually, through the development and acquisition of greater knowledge, the same cannot generally be said morally, especially of the young, who frequenting the great cities easily fall into vice and lose the good habits of religious virtue in which they had been brought up at home by their elders.”71

Don Tommaso Grilli ends his page on emigration by noting: “so it often happens that many families of this village sell their land to improve their situation and go and settle elsewhere”, referring in this connection to “Appendix B”, which it seems useful to reproduce, also because it directly concerns the family of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi.

The table suggests some observations: the number of those who moved increased markedly in the two decades after the unification of Italy; a third of them (12 out of 35) went elsewhere within the commune of Albareto or to the neighboring communes of Borgotaro and Compiano; next come Parma and the lowlands of Parma (five cases in all) and the hills of Piacenza (which include Centovera, in the commune of San Giorgio in the Nure valley, where Sister Anna del Salvatore’s father settled), with four cases.

Health conditions

8. - Don Tommaso Grilli gives brief notes on the epidemics of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries:

- in 1737 “there was a serious epidemic that struck young and old. It began with a slow inflammation of the chest, followed by an acute and fatal fever, so that in that year, as can be seen from the death registers, 42 adults died in this parish”;

- in 1815 “typhus also broke out, and 52 adults died in Albareto”;

- in 1855 “cholera appeared for the first time and wrought havoc in almost all the parishes of the Commune, and the dead were buried here and there in their own fields. Many in Albareto were affected, but no one died”;73

- in 1867 “cholera returned and wrought havoc in the neighboring villages. In Albareto, of many who fell ill, only three died”;

- in 1873 “diphtheria came, attacking mainly children. In Albareto 63 people died”;

- in 1885 “in September there were a few sporadic cases of cholera in Albareto, while in Borgotaro it was wreaking havoc and markets and fairs were canceled”.74

According to Cenni Storici di Albareto, the local municipal medical service was entrusted from 1870 onwards first to Dr Giuseppe Alpi of Compiano; in the following years the doctor changed frequently (1874, Dr Dal Lago of Pomarance and then Dr Fattori; 1879, Dr Bernardi of Compiano; 1882, Dr Bonardi for Albareto and Compiano, resident in Compiano; 1886, Dr Antonio Leonardi of Borgotaro, acting); finally, in 1888 the post was given to Dr Domenico Gotelli (1860-1946), whose more than forty years of service would be long remembered in the Gotra valley and surrounding area.75

Mussi summarizes the social and health situation in the upper Taro valley as follows (though in fact referring specifically to Borgotaro):

“Child mortality from birth to five years is about 30 [per cent] of births and accounts for almost half of all deaths. The commune helps, as far as its means allow, with 5 lire a month [about 30,000 lire today] for mothers who cannot breastfeed and whose families are destitute. The commune’s medical service is provided by two municipal doctors, whose care is by law free for the poor. There is a hospital in Borgotaro which, owing to its financial straits, does not admit chronic illnesses. There are no infant schools, either rural or in town, which, though many would like them, could not be set up for lack of funds. There are no mutual aid societies among the peasants.”76

Education

9. - Molossi, a writer certainly not hostile to the ducal government and to Archduchess Marie Louise, noted that

“the state of public instruction and education is not, truth to tell, as encouraging, considering the population as a whole, as it is among other civilized peoples.”77

He added that

“the really excessive difficulty of finding capable teachers78 means that not all communes can have a primary school, or at least teaching in all three classes. It is hoped that this defect will gradually disappear, and that a favorable opportunity will arise to provide for the education of girls of the lowest classes, that of the higher classes having made great progress in recent years.”

Under the ducal decrees of 1831, “primary schools for boys” should have been established in all communes; in fact, a report by the Magistrate in charge of public education shows that in 1833, in eleven communes including Albareto, teaching was entrusted to the parish priests by way of exception.79

Primary education lasted three years, during which “neither more than 400 nor fewer than 320 lessons may be given”; each “lesson” lasted two hours, divided between morning and afternoon, making a total of 160 to 200 school days of four hours each.

Classes were often large; teachers were few and poorly paid;80 curricula were inadequate;81 police interference in school matters (especially the appointment of “teachers”) was heavy-handed;82 even relying on parish priests, at least according to Poggi, did not improve the situation:

“The most general and effective remedy was in the end to encourage the parish priests to take charge of elementary education, although they had not yet lost the habit of beating the boys and keeping them on their knees for hours on end.”83

The time frame of Don Tommaso Grilli’s Manipolo di Cognizioni... is half a century later, and the picture it paints has changed considerably:

“By virtue of the laws of the present government,” he writes, “a boys’ elementary school was set up in Albareto at the expense of the municipal administration, in which girls are now also taught. In winter, for several years, evening classes were held for adults. The number of illiterates in the rising generation has greatly decreased. Parents should take greater care to make their children attend, and attendance should be encouraged with prizes for study.”84

The establishment of municipal schools, however, did not take place without resistance from local administrators.85

At the end of 1869 a Decree was issued urging the establishment of municipal schools run by qualified teachers and granting a subsidy of 500 lire, the annual salary of a teacher (about 3,400,000 lire today); the mayor and council decided, however, in May 1870, to postpone the matter and leave the school “in the hands of the Parish Priests or of whoever offers and is considered sufficiently fit to teach”. Among the reasons given were the difficulty for the children of getting to school (“this commune is crossed by many streams which in winter, in rain or when the snow melts, are quite impassable, since not one of them has a bridge”); the wish to avoid arousing “jealousies and quarrels” between the place where the school was set up and the other localities of the commune; the rejection of a single school for boys and girls, which would not have been moral; and above all the impossibility, after what had happened with the “milling tax”, of raising the “hearth tax”, a measure essential to meet the costs of opening the school.

In November of the same year, faced with the prefecture’s requests to open schools in five comunelli (Albareto, Campi, Folta, Montegroppo, San Quirico), the Council decided to leave “elementary education in the hands of the parish priests, with the obligation to prepare the young people for the school examination before a special commission, since no other provision can be made”.

Only in July 1871 were two boys’ schools opened, one at Costello di Albareto and the other at Folta; the teachers were appointed in November.

A year later, in November 1872, the municipal Council granted 300 lire to Campi and Pieve di Campi to set up an elementary school; in 1876 the establishment of two mixed schools was approved, one at Montegroppo and the other at Roncole for Gotra and Buzzò.

Teachers changed rather frequently, sometimes because the municipal Council decided to dismiss a teacher who was too negligent; until 1881, in any case, the Council appointed the local parish priests as “superintendents of schools”.86

“In former times,” Don Tommaso Grilli also recalls, “there were always private schools run by the parish priest or other priests. They taught reading, writing and arithmetic limited to the simplest calculations; not Italian grammar but Latin, mainly to those who wished to go on to the priesthood.”87

This last remark leads us to mention a church institution founded around the middle of the nineteenth century at Bedonia, a historic parish of the diocese of Piacenza in the Taro valley about ten kilometers from Albareto, which was to have enormous importance not only in church life but also in the civil and cultural life of the whole Taro valley.

The Seminary of Bedonia

10. - In the first half of the nineteenth century, writes Mgr Bruno Perazzoli in his fine essay on the origins of the Seminary,88 “there already existed in Bedonia, probably founded by the local parish priest Don Tedaldi, a ‘Bedonia church school’”, which in 1846 was absorbed into the Seminary and which, thanks to the priests who ran it, gave the Taro valley many men of culture.

In 1835 this “church school” was entrusted to Don Giovanni Agazzi (1792-1864),89 who “devoted himself above all to the care and formation of those aspiring to the priesthood, who came not only from every part of the Taro valley but also from the dioceses of Parma, Pontremoli, Bobbio and Genoa”.90

The young men attending the “school” lodged in houses in the village, often living in attics and under stairs and eating food provided by their families.

This situation led the archpriest of Bedonia, Don Stefano Raffi (1786-1864), to plan a building to house the clerical students; when he put the project to Don Giovanni Agazzi, the latter immediately embraced the idea, which was promptly welcomed and approved by the Bishop of Piacenza, the Parmesan nobleman Mgr Luigi Sanvitale.

With his support and the enormous participation of the people of the upper Taro valley,91 the building was quickly completed and inaugurated on 25 July 1846 in the presence of Mgr Sanvitale and also of the Bishop of Pontremoli, Mgr Michelangelo Orlandi.

Sanvitale entrusted the direction of the Seminary to the Vincentian Missionaries founded by Saint Vincent de Paul (also called Lazarists or Priests of the Mission), who were already at the Alberoni College in Piacenza; the first rector was Fr. Giuseppe Bailo, a learned man in close contact with Antonio Rosmini, whose thought he introduced to Piacenza.

Those were particularly complex years politically and in relations between Church and States; Bishop Sanvitale and his vicar general, Mgr Antonio Silva of Bedonia,92 took a stance of broad openness to the changes that were coming [...].93

This stance found full agreement in Fr. Bailo and his confreres, as well as in the “teacher” Don Giovanni Agazzi;

“the teachers of the Seminary belonging to the Order of Lazarists, led by their Rector, a certain Bailo, a supporter of the Italian idea,” wrote a member of parliament from Bedonia, the left-wing radical Primo Lagasi, “using the influence they had gained in their two years there, helped to make this idea attractive and welcome to the people of the Taro and Ceno valleys, most of whom followed it.”94

A plebiscite for union with Piedmont was even organized and, despite the attempt by the ducal Dragoons stationed at Compiano to prevent it, was held on 18 April 1848 with the participation of the Seminary’s students and teachers too;95 Bedonia and 16 of the 23 parishes of its district voted for annexation to Piedmont.

As the general situation took an unfavorable turn, sanctions followed, culminating in the expulsion of the “Priests of the Mission” from Bedonia, carried out by the Dragoons manu militari on 30 August 1850; they never returned.

They were accused of Jansenism, Giobertism and secularist liberalism, charges firmly rebutted by Fr. Giovanni Rinaldi, also a fervent Rosminian, who had succeeded Fr. Bailo as rector of the Seminary.

Not everyone shared the Vincentian Fathers’ positions; there were therefore divisions, some of them painful, among the clergy, such as that between Don Giovanni Agazzi and Don Stefano Raffi, who remained loyal to the Duchy of Parma; relations between Bedonia on the one hand and Bardi and Borgotaro, which remained loyal to the Parma government, on the other also suffered.96

Bedonia is in the diocese of Piacenza and Albareto in the diocese of Pontremoli; yet it seemed appropriate to mention these events briefly, since they show how lively the church circles of Bedonia were in the mid-nineteenth century, and because, as has already emerged, they had a wide influence throughout the upper Taro valley, beyond the boundaries of church districts.

Aspects of religious tradition and practice

11. - At Boschetto, less than two kilometers from the parish church of Albareto, going up the flat floor of the Gotra valley, stands the Sanctuary of the Blessed Virgin Mary, commemorating a miraculous event in 1683, when a deaf-mute shepherd girl, Angela Broglia, while praying before an image of Our Lady painted on a stone, regained her hearing and speech. An Oratory was built on the spot by Maffeo Bontii, then Commissioner of the Farnese at Borgotaro, in thanksgiving for a “grace of healing” he received there, perhaps in 1684; the oratory was blessed and dedicated on 9 June 1686 and soon became a place of devotion and pilgrimage, especially for the annual feast of the Holy Name of Mary; on 23 February 1685 Innocent XI had granted a plenary indulgence to visitors to the oratory who fulfilled the usual conditions.97

As we shall see, however, some, like Don Giovanni Maestri, parish priest of Albareto in the mid-nineteenth century, gave a different and much less comforting interpretation of the local people’s attendance at this oratory: that of a Sunday Mass without a “sermon”, quicker than the parish Mass.

Nevertheless, this is one sign of a tenacious and widespread popular religiosity, which harsh living conditions, extreme frugality, hard daily sacrifices, constant familiarity with death and long tradition fostered and encouraged, as we shall see in examining the documents on pastoral visitations, among the people of Albareto and of these mountains more generally.

“The people,” writes Don Tommaso Grilli, perhaps with a touch of indulgence, “are of sober habits and a gentle, sociable disposition; cases of immorality are rare and severely condemned by public opinion. Simple but lasting affection almost always goes with marriage. The inhabitants lead an active and frugal life and have good, deep-rooted religious habits. They work the land with perseverance and diligence. In general they are thrifty and industrious, not very fond of amusements, but rather eager to acquire landed property.”98

There are some criticisms:

“Some ignorant people,” Don Tommaso notes shortly afterwards, “are also superstitious, especially in illness, using cabbalistic signs to cure it”99

and again:

“There are still those who consider certain days unlucky for certain actions, and many also blame the new moon for many ills.”100

Another indicator of widespread religiosity, though not unconnected with the overall socio-economic picture,101 is the large number of priests born there.

In the course of the nineteenth century Albareto had five parish priests: in 1796 Don Giuseppe Carlo Bosi was appointed rector, succeeded on 1 January 1802 by Don Lodovico Bosi, who remained for 37 years, until 1839; after a short interim with the administrator Don Luigi Lanzarotti, Don Giovanni Maestri came in 1840 and was rector for 19 years;102 he was succeeded in 1859, first as administrator and then as rector, by Don Tommaso Grilli, our Author, who, as we have said, remained for 64 years, until 1923.103

Many other priests, however, came from Albareto in the nineteenth century; several are mentioned in the answers to the questionnaires prepared for pastoral visitations.

It may also be recalled that in the census taken by Don Lodovico Bosi in 1821, mentioned above, eight other priests besides the parish priest were living in the parish of Albareto at that time.

Don Grilli gives a list of priests from the parish of Albareto who died between 1748 and 1890: there are 43 of them.104

In 1893, again according to Don Grilli, 17 priests born in Albareto were living;105 all but one belonged to the secular clergy and worked mainly in parishes of the Gotra valley and the diocese of Piacenza.

Fr. Angelo Sabini (Albareto, 7 December 1854 - Turin, 21 February 1896), brother of Antonio and Andrea, also priests, had instead joined the Missionaries of Saint Vincent de Paul on 27 September 1876; he died twenty years later with a reputation for holiness.

Don D. O. Schiavetta concludes the pages devoted to Fr. Angelo by observing that

“he certainly knew [Sister Anna del Salvatore] here on earth, since there seem to have been ties of kinship and friendship with her brothers Luigi and Giovanni, who also studied at Bedonia. Moreover, Sister Anna will have told him about the great figure of Fr. G. Battista Tornatore, her spiritual director, a priest of the Mission; it was probably no coincidence that Don Angelo Sabini also joined that Congregation.”106

Cenni Storici di Albareto also gives the names of 24 women religious born in the commune of Albareto between 1842 (the year Marianna Orsi, Sister Anna del Salvatore, was born) and 1949; it is remarkable that several religious vocations in the same family were not uncommon: we have just mentioned the Sabini brothers; the same applies to the family of Sister Anna del Salvatore, to the three Tomaselli sisters, Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, and to many others.

The sacrifices made by such a poor population for the upkeep of their churches and chapels are also, as we saw in the case of the Seminary of Bedonia, a significant sign of popular religiosity.

During the nineteenth century the people of Albareto rebuilt the parish church because “the old church was too small for the increased population”; this took place between 1843 and 1857.110 “Everything was done at the people’s expense, as the inscription on the façade shows: ‘Gentis Albareti sumptu pietate labore’” (by the expense, piety and labor of the people of Albareto), Don Tommaso points out, going on at length about its finishing and the craftsmen who did the work.

“In 1865 the presbytery was almost entirely rebuilt, more decently arranged than the old one, which was no more than a rustic hovel [some details on this will be given shortly], and with greater comfort inside.”

In 1866 it was the turn of the four bells, cast at Casale di Albareto by Giovanni Capanni of Castelnuovo Monti; the largest bears the inscription: “Aenea voce loquor ne gentis Albareti pietas ulli lateat” (I speak with a voice of bronze so that the piety of the people of Albareto may be hidden from none).

Then came the cemetery: “in 1872-73 the walls of the said cemetery were rebuilt, the original ones having deteriorated”, with the sturdy iron entrance gate supported by square pillars “built of stone entirely worked with the chisel”:

“the cost,” notes Don Tommaso, who was responsible for some of this work, having become parish priest in 1859, “was borne by the Administration of the Comunalie of this community, with the consent of the people.”111

Notes from pastoral visitations

12. - Interesting documents on religious practice in Albareto in the nineteenth century survive in the questionnaires filled in by the parish priests in preparation for pastoral visitations and in the records of the visitations themselves. Albareto, an outlying parish reachable from Pontremoli (and even more so, before 1853, from Sarzana) only by a long and tiring journey across the mountains, was not included in every visitation; but we still have, in Sarzana, Don Stefano Bosi’s answers to the questions posed by Mgr Giulio Cesare Lomellini in 1790 and the record of the visitation of 5 May 1840 by Mgr Francesco Agnini,112 and in Pontremoli the documents relating to the visitations of 1856, 1875 and 1891.

For several reasons the answers given by the parish priest Don Giovanni Maestri, then 57 and in charge of the parish for 17 years, to the “questions” put to him in preparation for the visitation of 26 June 1856 are particularly interesting for our purposes; it was the first visitation after the parish of Albareto had been transferred to the Diocese of Pontremoli, carried out by a particularly authoritative bishop, Mgr Michele Angiolo Orlandi (1793-1874; Bishop of Pontremoli from 1839 until his death),113 when Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi was 14. These answers are thus a snapshot which, however subjective and “interested”, captures the state of religious practice locally at precisely the time Sister Anna lived there.

The nineteenth century in Albareto: between tradition and modernization

13. - The nineteenth century announced itself, even in the remote (but not so remote) upper Taro valley, with the din of the French armies; the most vivid description of those sad events is by Don Antonio Emmanueli, who certainly loved neither the French nor Napoleon; he writes:

“When [the Duke of Parma and Piacenza, Don Ferdinand of Bourbon] died on 9 October 1802, his son Louis should have succeeded him, but the French republic had sent him off to Etruria, where he survived his father by only seven months. We became subjects of France, and these villages of ours, which had been attached administratively to the twenty-eighth military division of the empire based in Genoa, and directly to the department of the Apennines with its prefecture in Chiavari and sub-prefecture in Pontremoli, had to shed very bitter tears.

These events are faithfully recorded in the archive of the parish of Albareto.

On 8 January 1806, by order of the Commander of the French Troops, all the weapons and ammunition of the inhabitants of these Villages had to be handed over within 24 hours, those who disobeyed being liable to arrest and trial by a military Commission in Genoa [...].

In that year the first military conscription was held. Many young men evaded this and later call-ups, but afterwards almost all were forced to obey under great threats and harassment. Many died in the various battles, and some came home [...].

Several times that year the government authorities ordered the Parish Priests to celebrate great festivities, now for the anniversary of the Coronation of Emperor Napoleon, now for the glorious victories won on the Rhine. Thus this government, when it wished, also donned the robes of the Prefect of the Congregation of Sacred Rites.”116

Many other “novelties” would follow these upheavals at the beginning of the century; some of them, concerning fundamental aspects of political and social life such as emigration and education, have already been mentioned; many others are carefully recorded by Don Tommaso Grilli in his writings. Some concern small everyday things: thus he notes that “after the year 1842 no more wolves were seen, which formerly often terrified shepherds and flocks”, or “that after the middle of this century people here began to use postage stamps to send letters”; he records changes in men’s and women’s dress, or the spread of smoking, “almost the fashion that a man is more important if he has a pipe or a cigar in his mouth”.

A prominent place in his notes is given, however, to the technical innovations that closely affected the valley: thus “in 1883-84 the bridge over the Taro at Campi was built, and Luigi Dorà, son of Domenico, of Albareto, assisted in running the steam pumps during the excavation and construction of the piers”; at about the same time work began on boring the Borgallo tunnel for the Parma-La Spezia railway, a project completed ten years later, in 1893: on 28 May Don Tommaso notes that “the Borgallo mountain was pierced and it was a day of great celebration”; the railway was opened the following year; in 1895 “a cableway was built from Borgotaro [railway] station to the Lagaccio in the mountains of Albareto to carry wood and charcoal”.117

Nor is there a lack of reference to the tensions caused by the milling tax; thus, under the year 1869, Don Tommaso records:

“On 12 January, when the law of 7 July 1868 on milling came into force, an extraordinary and reprehensible riot took place in this Commune, to the alarm of sensible people, which for brevity I will not describe. After this uprising a company of Bersaglieri was immediately sent from Parma; they were stationed in Albareto and set up their headquarters in Signora Caterina Celli’s summer house to prevent further gatherings and to enforce the milling tax, remaining there for a month. Then the boldest became the most timid and, without any further public sign of opposition, paid for all the turns that the mechanical counters recorded in the milling of their grain until 1 January 1884, when that law ceased.”118

As can be seen, many things were changing deep in the lives of the people of the Gotra valley and of these mountains; Don Antonio Emmanueli, a man of wide culture who took an active part in the events of his time, reflected on these changes in those years with heartfelt pessimism.119

The great wave of cultural, political, economic and technological change had by then fully swept over these lands which, though never static nor cut off from other places near and far, had for centuries preserved a strong, if harsh, identity of their own, of which a deep-rooted popular religiosity was undoubtedly a defining feature.

Since then, at an ever-increasing pace, many other things have changed, but even today that identity cannot be said to have been entirely lost.
