Against this background a positive factor emerges besides the religious and moral life of the people of Albareto: what nature offered, for, as Don Grilli also writes, “because of its position, the pleasantness of the place and the healthy air, (the village) is rightly considered one of the most delightful places to stay in the valley”.

The various pieces of information available help us to reconstruct, at least in broad outline, the life of the Servant of God in her native place before she moved away and entered religious life. This information, still vividly remembered by local people, is moreover confirmed by the witnesses who swore de veritate dicenda at the Process on the basis of what they had learned from their forebears rather than from books. Nor is it the usual information, certainly true but blurred by the passage of time and reduced to general and never contradicted testimonies of piety and virtue, as sometimes happens with other Servants of God whose light, spread at a later period, is reflected back on their early years, which were differently illustrated but, as far as is known, without negative traits. Here, by contrast, the reputation for holiness arising from Marianna Orsi’s merits (we are still speaking of her early years) is not conditioned by the reputation she herself would later acquire when, before, during and after the painful trials she overcame and through her constant practice of the virtues up to and beyond the limit of sacrifice, they showed themselves in continual progress along the narrow, thorny path she set out on while still very young.

Albareto in the nineteenth century was not a rich village, nor were the Orsi among the most prosperous families there, though frugality, work in the fields, seasonal emigration and later, for most, permanent emigration to the United States from the second half of the century could soften the harshness of poverty.

The great strength of those people was their faith and their lively and heartfelt observance of Christian morality:

“The people,” Don Grilli writes again, “are of sober habits and a gentle, sociable disposition; cases of immorality are rare and severely condemned by public opinion. Simple but lasting affection almost always goes with marriage.

The inhabitants lead an active and frugal life and have good, deep-rooted habits.

They work the land with perseverance and diligence. In general they are thrifty and industrious, not very fond of amusements, but rather eager to acquire landed property.

After their housework the women work in the fields and at farm tasks as much as the men; they have many children and sometimes twins. Few are obliged to remain unmarried against their will.”120

In that setting and with many of those characteristics lived the family of Angelo Orsi and Domenica Mussi.

Both of Marianna’s parents came from old families rooted in Albareto, where members had also held church and civil offices.

The Orsi were already known at the beginning of the seventeenth century, and there is a record of the death in 1621 of some members of the family, struck by pestilential fevers that appeared with “pain, that is, pleurisy” in the house of Antonio Orsi, causing the death of this worthy man, his wife Giovanna, his son Francesco (already an adult) and his brother Michele.121

The seventeenth-century parish records also contain favorable mentions of priests of the family, whose succession is known from that century onwards.

For seventeen years, from 1663 to 1680, Don Giovanni Antonio Orsi122 was rector of the parish church of Albareto, where priests of the same family later served, namely Bernardo (1691-1748), Stefano I (1710-1764), Stefano II (1740-1802), Angelo (1809-1815) and Andrea (1754-1816),123 while Domenico I (1750-1822) was rector of Cacciarasca and Stefano III (1777-1850) of Campi. Don Domenico II (1753-1844) remained in Albareto, and his nephew of the same name (1784-1855) became a canon of the collegiate church of San Secondo; there were also Angelo (1822-1878), pro-vicar of Le Fontanelle;124 Giovanni (born 10 October 1801 and still living in 1893), administrator of Caroseto (San Polo); and Valentino (born 1861), administrator of Pracchiola.125

As can be seen, every generation was blessed with a priest, and sometimes more than one; and two of Marianna Orsi’s brothers, as we shall see, attended the Seminary of Bedonia, though without becoming priests.126

Her mother’s family too had given priests to the local Church since the seventeenth century, at almost the same rate as the Orsi: Pellegrino Mussi was administrator of Albareto from 15 May to 26 September 1680,127 while Marco I (1710-1754) held the same office in his home parish before becoming chaplain at Gattico. Among the clergy of Albareto were Paolo (1681-1771), Giuseppe I (1707-1785) and Giuseppe II (1732-1810); Marco II (1775-1863) was rector of Lozzola;128 Antonio (1818-1890) and the Servant of God’s maternal uncle, Don Luigi, born in 1827 and still living in 1893, held the same office at Roccalanzona and Codogno respectively.129

In civil life there were the mayor Francesco Mussi from 1814 and the mayor Lorenzo from 1863.130

The day after her birth (not the same day, since Marianna was born at eight in the evening on 22 February 1842) the baby was taken to the parish baptistery, where the rector administered the Sacrament of Baptism, her godfather being her uncle Francesco Mussi and her godmother her paternal aunt Giovanna, daughter of Domenico Orsi.131

For the birth of Marianna, the eldest of nine children, there was a “great celebration” at home, following the celebration the Church had made for the new creature reborn to Grace through the Sacrament. The Servant of God’s first biographer mentions other reasons for the joy shown by her fortunate parents:

“But if the father was happy at the birth of his first child,” it was written, “the mother could not contain her joy, so great was it, and she showed it to the relatives and friends who came to visit her, telling everyone that she was completely happy and had nothing left to wish for here below.”132

All this seems very natural and spontaneous: a family like the Orsi, remembered by all as deeply religious, could not but rejoice at the birth of a child to be brought up in the fear of God, for whom every parent hopes for growth in virtue and the attainment of eternal salvation. But we must consider what the Servant of God’s first biographer writes; unfortunately she does not give her sources, but since so many people were still alive at the time, both in her native village and among the Daughters of Saint Anne (including Marianna’s sister), she could not have said anything untrue, and indeed what she says was well known to many.

At that time Sister Anna del Salvatore’s mother was still alive, and probably either from her or from her daughter Sister Anna Fabiana the first biographer learned of the mother’s presentiment, which she reports with a credible hypothesis as to the origin of such joy:

“I could not say for sure, but I know that the birth of this little girl brought her parents such great joy that they themselves could never explain it, and they certainly never felt the like at the birth of any other child of their large family.”133

After Marianna, two more girls and six boys brightened the Orsi home, all welcomed with joy and brought up with love.

Local tradition has nothing but good to say of Marianna and her early years, and the testimonies at the Process confirm the biographers’ view of her exemplary childhood.

14. - The testimonies about the Servant of God’s early years are not very numerous, but they are precise and reliable. Her sister, Sister Anna Fabiana, agrees with them; recalling some details of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s family life, she told the Provincial, who later testified at the Process in Palermo, “that even at that (childhood) age the Servant of God showed something special in her piety and devotion; a retired and mortified life”.134

When in 1846 the Bishop of Pontremoli, Mgr Michele Angelo Orlandi, gave her the Sacrament of Confirmation during his pastoral visit to Albareto, Marianna, though very young, felt and understood the sacred rite as “a truly extraordinary event”. Again according to local tradition, never denied or altered, the four-year-old girl, “though she had not yet reached the age of reason, by the devotion with which she came to receive this Sacrament gave clear signs of understanding its full importance”.135

Her regular attendance at the parish priest’s Christian Doctrine classes and the profit she drew from them, as she already had from her parents’ teaching, earned Marianna the privilege of being admitted very early, contrary to the custom of the time, to the Eucharistic Table.

The biographer dwells on various details of that day, again without giving the source; but the precise references suggest that some witness well qualified to speak of it informed the writer. The account, fully credible in the light of other testimonies, reads:

“The day of her first Communion was a day of bliss for her. She already felt drawn to her Divine Spouse, who was later to be the treasure, comfort and hope of this pure soul.”

Is this the logic of post hoc, ergo propter hoc? We think not, given the biographer’s further detail about that moment of grace:

“To be edified one had to see with what devotion this remarkable girl, kneeling with joined hands, waited for the priest to bring the Sacred Host to her lips, which trembled with inner emotion! Other girls had shared this heavenly grace with her, but on no other face could one see, as on hers, such ardent desire to possess Jesus and such deep fear of being unworthy to receive the King of kings.”136

Also because of the upbringing she had received and the Christian life of her family, Marianna felt ever more attached and grateful to her mother; though there is very little evidence on this point, a letter from Sister Anna del Salvatore to Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno sheds more light on her feelings of filial devotion than many words and digressions could. The letter, dated Palermo, 20 December 1881, reads:

“Dearest Mother, for the first time I venture to ask you a favor, and it is this: one day a lady paid me the monthly fee and then gave me 20 francs, saying: ‘Take these twenty francs and give them to the poor’; so I ask you whether I might send them to my mother, because I know for certain, indeed [I am] quite sure, that she is not very well at present!… What do you say? Dear Mother, rather than giving them to other poor people…”137

Further confirmation comes from a document by Don Giuseppe Giacopazzi, who had questioned the parish priest of Albareto; he gives more information “without adding or removing anything”, including the testimony of the Servant of God’s mother (“I will only tell you that she was always a good girl”) and this further reference to the virtues she practized while still living with her family:

“Her mother Domenica Mussi, who is still living in Piacenza,” wrote Don Giacopazzi on 4 December 1890, “assures me that this daughter never once caused her sorrow. Indeed she told me that sometimes, when she was still very small, she found her up at night praying. For the rest, even she cannot tell me anything that smacks of the heroic.”138

It is possible that on her frequent journeys to Piacenza in connection with her mission the Servant of God obtained the Foundress’s permission to visit her elderly mother; but apart from her grief at a brother’s death and her living with her sister Sister Anna Fabiana in Rome and Palermo,139 we know nothing more about her continued relations with her family.

It was in this setting that Marianna Orsi’s virtues showed themselves very early, and Don Tommaso Grilli, with sure knowledge of the facts, attested to Sister Anna Fabiana in a letter of 5 April 1913 her sister’s “good and religious conduct”, giving a detailed account and also stating that:

“She received the Holy Sacraments devoutly and said her prayers devoutly; she attended novenas and feasts, even those of devotion only. When needed, she never failed to carry a light accompanying the Holy Viaticum to the sick and the bodies of the dead to their resting place.

This parishioner of mine (I say parishioner because when she left Albareto I had been parish priest for 6 years) was a young woman of gentle character and calm spirit, without vanity in dress or behavior, sincere and cheerful but modest in conversation with her companions, obedient and respectful. With praiseworthy patience she bore the lack of things she often needed. Being the eldest, she helped her mother with great care and patience in bringing up and minding her little brothers and sisters. In this she was certainly always a great relief and help to her mother through the exercise of her charity.”140

The same virtues, in the same words, were attested by her uncle Lorenzo Mussi, also referring to the time the Servant of God spent at home; among other things he attributed to his niece’s intercession a rapid and complete recovery from pleurisy and pneumonia.141

The Servant of God’s first biographer also stresses the work she did within the family, especially in caring for the upbringing of her brothers and sisters, who were very often entrusted to her and for whom she gave up even the innocent amusements of her age.

We read in the Cenni storici:

“And when they committed faults for which their mother would have had to punish them, there was their loving sister defending them against their mother’s just severity, asking forgiveness for them and offering herself as surety for their future conduct. And since with her fine discernment she well understood that nothing is more harmful in bringing up children than ill-advised pity and indulgence, sensible little thing that she was, while she pleaded for her little brothers with their mother, she became a strict judge when she was alone with them, doing her duty by admonishing them for the faults for which she had just begged forgiveness.”142

These may not seem great things, but her constant application to works of piety and mercy, her forgetfulness of self for the good of others and her flowering in virtues, hidden or manifest, foreshadowed in that domestic serenity the other expressions of her spirit, especially in painful and difficult moments, when her only comfort was the Christ of Golgotha, to whom Sister Anna del Salvatore entrusted her innocence and defense.

Returning to her early years, Marianna’s exemplary virtue is universally attested by local tradition, which remains alive to this day. On 16 June 1998 Signora Bice Borella of Albareto, owner of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s birthplace, testified under oath at the supplementary Inquiry of the Process on the life, virtues and reputation for holiness of the Servant of God as follows:

“I learned from my parents that Sister Anna del Salvatore, even in winter, would kneel and, defying the cold, pray for a long time on the bare floor. We too, from childhood, prayed and remembered Sister Anna del Salvatore because ‘she was really good,’ they told us, ‘more than an ordinary nun’! […].

In past years, around 1950-1954, I remember that some people took away ‘as relics’ a few small pieces of the wooden floor of the room where the Servant of God was born.”143

The next day the archiepiscopal delegate for the Cause of Beatification, Don Giorgio Scimeca, drew up this report on the condition of the Servant of God’s birthplace:

“I declare that on 17.06.1998, together with the promoter of justice [Don Giuseppe Oliveri] and the notary actuary [Don Anselmo Lipari], I visited the birthplace of the said Servant of God at ‘Le Moie’, a hamlet about a kilometer from Albareto (Parma). It is a dwelling that has undergone modernization of the ceiling, floor and plastering of the walls. Surviving from that time are the dressed-stone staircase to the upper floor and the doors with their frames.

The members of the tribunal were received by the present owner of the house, Signora Bice Borella, who showed us the room where the Servant of God was born.”144

In her small village, where nothing escaped people’s notice, the reputation for the virtues she showed while still in the world took root, and then spread and was handed down even among those who could not have known her; in particular, as the Process shows, “great emphasis was placed on the Servant of God’s life of poverty, sacrifice, prayer and work”.145 A former President of Catholic Action testified that she was always invoked in prayer, “because,” the witness added, “she was an example of life and because we always considered her a ‘saint’, a protector very close to us”.146

Nor have commemorative celebrations and prayers been neglected, to honor her, seek her intercession and hold her up as an example to all; “people take part in them very willingly”.147 Even today she is spoken of “both by the elderly and by an old parish priest”, who unanimously consider her an exemplary person. The same witness adds “that people said she was truly a saint”.148

Sister Anna Maria Eugenia Calderaro of the Daughters of Saint Anne (born Ermenegilda) did not hesitate to say:

“In Albareto I experienced what people say about the Servant of God and the devotion they live.

On the 150th anniversary of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s birth […] more than 18 of us Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne, experienced the ‘very strong devotion’ of her native village.”149

“She was spoken of in our family,” said a distant niece, Renata Ponti of Genoa, who also had an aunt among the Daughters of Saint Anne. “I have always kept a photograph of her, and when my mother [Domitilla Belloglio] died, she urged us never to forget the memory of our aunt the nun. In the evening I pray for the beatification of Padre Pio and of Sister Anna del Salvatore.”

She had entrusted to her her husband, injured in an accident,

“so that he could walk, and now, thanks to her intercession, he is as he was before […] So far,” the witness continued, “I have not yet visited her tomb, but I hope at least to visit the house in Albareto where the Servant of God was born.”150

Again regarding the house where Sister Anna del Salvatore was born and spent her early years, Maria Tomaselli, aged eighty, drawing on her distant memories, stated:

“An aunt of mine used to say to me, pointing out the house in Albareto where Sister Anna del Salvatore was born and grew up: ‘A saint was born here.’ And the same aunt regarded the room where the nun was born almost as a chapel.”151

Professor Don Paolo Tommaselli, parish priest of Albareto since 1961, confirming the absence of forms of cult not permitted by the Church, added:

“Since 1992 a special ‘devotion’ to the Servant of God has developed in my parish community, and every day we say the prayer for her beatification. In particular we celebrate the anniversary of her birth (the first Sunday of February), often in the presence of the Bishop or the Vicar General.”152

And the parish priest of San Quirico, Don Duilio Odoidio Schiavetta, then in his sixties, confirmed the devout memory left by the Servant of God and handed down through the generations, with “oral testimonies [he had] collected since childhood” in Borgo Val di Taro, where Sister Anna del Salvatore was “much invoked during the last world war, and especially during the round-up on Good Friday 1944 in the Albareto area”.153

15. - Having reached what is now called “school age”, Marianna should have learned at least to read and a little writing and arithmetic, but in her village (and not only there) public education was not then provided for boys, still less for girls.

In time, but very slowly, things improved, and when Marianna had already left her village there was set up there, by government order and at the commune’s expense,

“a boys’ elementary school (…) in which,” as Don Grilli wrote in the 1890s, “girls are now also taught. In winter, for several years, evening classes were held for adults. The number of illiterates in the rising generation has greatly decreased. Parents should take greater care to make their children attend and encourage them with prizes for study.”

So wrote that parish priest, adding that in the past, that is, in Marianna Orsi’s girlhood, the only teaching, given privately by priests, was limited at the lower level to reading, writing and the simplest calculations, while at the higher level Latin grammar was taught, “mainly to those who wished to go on to the clerical life”. The young men’s education was of course completed in the seminary so that they could receive the major and minor Orders.154

Girls were therefore long excluded, and while for boys the indifference and needs of their families led them to neglect even the opportunity of free public schooling, very few parents bothered to have their daughters educated. This continued into the twentieth century, as shown by the testimony of illiterate ex auditu witnesses heard in the Supplementary Inquiry of the Servant of God’s Beatification Process, concluded on 16 May 2000.

But within the limits of what was needed for the rural economy of a small village, the Orsi were not negligent in this regard: they sent two sons to study at the Seminary of Bedonia and taught their eldest, Marianna, at home, and perhaps Fabiana too, of whose writing we also have examples in her letters, which are fairly correct in form.

Knowing his eldest daughter’s intelligence and eagerness to learn, Angelo Orsi wanted to make up for the lack of a public school (and, for girls, of the private one run by the parish clergy too), and became her teacher himself.

Given the state of education in the Duchy of Parma and the other Italian States, “not […], truth to tell, as encouraging, considering the population as a whole, as among other civilized peoples”,155 it might seem surprising that Marianna’s father was able to turn himself into a teacher, and one who, judging by his daughter’s writing, achieved his aim. But clearly father and daughter applied themselves to this too with the commitment typical of their people, good Christians above all and devoted to the good of others, persevering with will and tenacity on the path they had taken. A recent monograph on Albareto observes that

“it is precisely the capacity for sacrifice, self-denial and acceptance of death, instilled by the harshness of daily life, that built the basis of the Christian virtue and devotion to others found, especially in the past, among the people of our mountains.”156

With a barely adequate store of knowledge, but above all with the spirit of her people, which she embodied, Marianna, having made herself useful at home in looking after the children and working in the fields, accepted separation from the rest of the family to move to Bedonia with two of her brothers, Luigi and Giovanni, who had been admitted as day pupils at the diocesan Seminary.

If Marianna could not follow them in their studies, she certainly eased their hardships with the motherly care she gave them both.

We do not know much about the stay in Bedonia, except that in the single room they lived in, life was peaceful and poor. Marianna devoted herself to serving her brothers, “preparing their food, looking after their linen, keeping the house clean and guiding them, while their mother in Albareto saw to running the rest of the family”.

The first biographer added that:

“Having fulfilled this duty, she agreed to the wish of her uncles Don Antonio and Don Luigi Mussi, parish priests of Buzzò and Rovinaglia respectively, going now to one, now to the other, to keep house for them; but however happy she was with her uncles, who held her in the esteem she deserved, she could not get used to being separated from her mother and family, and decided to return to Albareto, where her character, behavior and the virtues she showed in the family and the parish made her ‘loved by the whole village’.”

And again:

“The seeds of religious feeling had taken deep root in her, and she received the Holy Sacraments with admirable devotion and consecrated to God the hours her household duties left her free. She hurried to Church for Novenas and feasts, as she hastened at the sound of the bell calling the faithful to accompany the Holy Viaticum to a sick person or a poor deceased person to their last resting place.”157

This information, favorable but unfortunately scanty, is corroborated by an unbroken tradition among local people and attests the spirit of obedience that Sister Anna del Salvatore would later cultivate in religious life. If we did not know the Servant of God’s humility, we might say that in her last words she could well have pointed to herself and her constant care for virtue as an example. Indeed in the funeral oration at her obsequies in Palermo the preacher recalled that when her confessor suggested to Sister Anna del Salvatore, then close to death, that she “leave her Daughters some keepsake, she made a supreme effort and said audibly: ‘Be good and obedient’”.158

She herself was the first to be good and obedient, even in the world, and especially when she had to part from her family once again; meanwhile, because of financial difficulties, the family was obliged to sell its property in Albareto and leave the village, hoping to rebuild a small fortune elsewhere. While her parents and brothers and sisters moved to Centovera near Piacenza, where her father died on 9 July 1867,159 Marianna was left in the village with her maternal uncles Francesco and Lorenzo Mussi, the latter mayor of Albareto, “as housekeeper, where thanks to her goodness she was loved and respected”.

Marianna stayed with those relatives for about three years and then rejoined her family, where she remained “until, called by God to the life of the cloister, she longed for nothing but to fulfill her desire”.

During this last period there was also a special moment for the Servant of God; the sources that mention it show how Marianna, honestly experiencing the attractions of the world without yielding to them, strengthened her resolve and gave a sure and final answer to her vocation.

Let us look at a long passage of the brief biography already cited:

“It was precisely for this reason [her desire for the cloister] that if, so as not to be rude or discourteous, she had to accept an invitation to some family party with friends or relatives, she came home disgusted and repentant, to the point of weeping when she was alone in the silence of her little room.

Likewise it was for this reason that, although at one time she had allowed someone to entertain hopes, who, attracted by her fine qualities, had asked her parents for her hand, she, enlightened by Grace from on high, later withdrew her word, saying that she no longer wished to marry because she felt drawn to become a nun. She did want a spouse, but one who would be ever beautiful, ever young, ever loving for all eternity. And what spouse could she mean but Jesus Christ?”160

Other testimonies, in another style, tell us of this crisis, if we may call it that; it seems that at first the suitor, Angelo Zecca, received an encouraging answer (“she is inclined to accept and, according to the custom of the time, gives him hope”); but called to a greater love, Marianna later told the young man in love with her of her different choice.161

Don Tommaso Grilli wrote to Sister Anna Fabiana:

“before entering religious life the Servant of God came back to Albareto to say goodbye to her relatives and friends, and had a friendly conversation with Signora Valentina Bosi of this parish, her confidante; she told her that she had found someone to marry and had given him hope, but that afterwards (certainly enlightened by grace from on high) she had thought it over and resolved to renounce the world, and had told the young man that she no longer wished to marry because she had decided to become a nun, thus choosing Jesus as her Spouse, as she later did.”162

If some noticed Marianna’s tears after attending a party, others testified, like Don Emilio Bosi, curate and deputy mayor of Albareto:

“Though I was a boy of about nine, I remember very well that the said Orsi, shortly before leaving Albareto, happened to be at my parents’ house one day during a family dance, and despite insistent invitations from those present to join in the fun, she always firmly refused.”163

16. - The Servant of God’s vocation had matured in prayer and sacrifice, and she persevered in it through the trials she underwent and the obstacles that stood in the way of fulfilling her inmost desire.

Prepared by a life entirely devoted to piety and the service of others, assiduous in receiving the Sacraments and always ready to face any sacrifice, Marianna was nevertheless also weighing her family duties, which had increased after her father’s death. We know very little about this period, but the first step Marianna took when she went to Piacenza with her sister Veronica (later Sister Anna Fabiana) suggests that her presence, though certainly wanted by the family, was no longer indispensable as before; nor is there any evidence of opposition from her mother or brothers. The only opposition came, if anything, from her priest uncles, as we shall see, and it did not concern any duties the Servant of God might have had towards her struggling family, but rather a certain skepticism about the Congregation she had chosen, which in their view offered no guarantee of stability.

This time the separation from her family would last not a few years but a lifetime. Marianna wondered about this future and entrusted herself completely to the Lord, waiting for it to be shown to her which way to go and to which institute she should turn for her vocation.

Until then Marianna had lived in the country or in small villages and seems to have had no contact with monasteries or religious congregations; she had devoted herself to housework, both at home and for devout priests such as the Bottego and Mussi; and while these praiseworthy experiences led her to look for a congregation of active life, at the same time, as she progressed spiritually, she could not remain insensitive to the call of contemplation.164

Amid these uncertainties Marianna learned of a new Institute founded (on 8 December 1866) in Piacenza itself, not many miles from Centovera, by Rosa Gattorno, who on 26 July 1867, the liturgical feast of Saint Anne, had herself taken the religious habit and assumed the name of the Mother of the Immaculate, placing it before her baptismal name. Because of this special devotion, all Daughters of Saint Anne still take this holy name today.

In one of the leaflets intended to make the new foundation known, the future Blessed and Fr. G. B. Tornatore, the Co-founder, had outlined the spirit of the Institute as follows:

“The specific purpose that distinguishes the Daughters of Saint Anne […] is to profess special devotion to glorious Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate […]. The Institute [professes] also, among other virtues, the compassion of the heart of Saint Anne, nursing the sick in their homes […].

Likewise they take in poor girls at risk, to preserve them from losing their innocence and virtue, and in this too they honor the care [Saint Anne] had for the Immaculate Child and the zeal the Saint must have had, through that care, to see all the young girls of the world innocent.”165

In the young woman from Albareto, who had been given at the font the names of the Immaculate Virgin and Saint Anne, these aims of charity towards others, especially the sick and young girls, must have found a full echo, even when, still unaware or at least not sufficiently informed of Mother Gattorno’s aims and works, she was wondering about her vocation.

“But someone,” we read in the latest biography devoted to her, “tells her that an Institute has recently been founded in Piacenza that devotes itself to the care of the sick and has shown truly heroic charity in nursing cholera victims during the recent epidemic; they also suggest that she go to the Alberoni College in the city and approach Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, the saint, who can introduce her to the foundress.”166

This man of God, after meeting Mother Rosa Gattorno (March 1866), had entered fully into the project of the Congregation, so much so that the Daughters of Saint Anne later recognized him as Co-founder. A Priest of the Mission, he lived at the Alberoni College in Piacenza, a higher school of theology; his wide and deep learning ranged over Sacred Scripture, moral theology and law, and his life had earned him the name of “saint” mentioned above.

Don Anselmo Lipari, his biographer, describes him as:

“A man particularly versed in the things of the Lord and passionate about his vocation: a person who lived his specific calling to the full, zealous for the worship of God and versed in the science of the Spirit. An excellent judge of the human heart, he willingly and very generously advised Mother Rosa, sacrificed himself for the new Institute and became so involved in her cause that he took on a role that was in some respects irreplaceable.”167

Marianna Orsi, as can be seen, had gone to the right person to test her vocation as a Daughter of Saint Anne when, accompanied by her sister Veronica, later Anna Fabiana, she went to the devout priest. He received them both kindly, but the frail figure of the Servant of God, already so worn by constant sacrifices and voluntary penances, made him fear that she would not be able to bear the fatigue and hardships of religious life, especially the life the Daughters of Saint Anne already led in caring for the sick, keeping night vigils and practizing the strict poverty of the new Institute.

Marianna was not daunted by the difficulties. To the arguments Fr. Tornatore put to her, as if to convince her that she was physically unfit to bear hardship and privation, she replied simply and firmly: “When I can no longer hold out with my body, I will hold out with my spirit.”

The devout Vincentian missionary, surprised by such humility and readiness for sacrifice, was suddenly convinced of the seriousness of her purpose, the fruit not of a generous impulse or momentary enthusiasm but solely of the Lord’s grace at work in her. So he did not hesitate to introduce her to Mother Rosa.168

We know nothing more about the meeting with Fr. Tornatore, but knowing his thinking and the Institute’s guidelines, we can quote here the definition of the tasks entrusted to the Daughters of Saint Anne, which he surely also explained to the young Marianna:

“The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, commonly called ‘nurses’, devotes itself to the good of others in the following works: first, home nursing of the sick of both sexes, by day and by night, whatever the illness. The nurses give their care without taking anything from the sick person, not even a drop of coffee. They also take on the care of Hospitals. They always go to nurse in pairs. Second, they take poor girls at risk off the streets, that is, girls who, having no one to look after them, are in danger of losing their virtue; they educate them by having them live with them; and they also run schools for little boys up to the age of twelve.”169

On 4 November 1868 Marianna entered the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne as a postulant.170

Eleven days later the parish priest of Centovera, Don Felice Tedaldi, wrote a brief certificate of “excellent conduct and irreproachable morals”.171 Of this conduct of the Servant of God, constant throughout her life, we have among other testimonies that of Don Domenico Pizzoli, parish priest of San Nicolò dell’Albergheria (Palermo), who in the eulogy placed on 14 February 1887 in the coffin in which Sister Anna del Salvatore was buried managed, despite the florid prose of the time, to sum up the charism of the Servant of God, faithful unto death to her Institute, “whose spirit is none other than to serve God by serving one’s neighbor”, and her conduct, which was “an example to her sisters and an edification to her superiors”.172

Less than five months after entering, the young Orsi was admitted to the novitiate and took the name of Sister Anna del Salvatore.173

Although there is not much information about the Servant of God’s first years among the Daughters of Saint Anne, there are enough testimonies to prove her love for and observance of the Rule and her promptness in fulfilling her duties, especially in the practice of charity, in which the special virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore came to light, in her own personal style, in humility and in a constant outpouring of love for God and neighbor.

The praise given her for what she did certainly goes beyond general approval and constitutes genuine historical testimony, characterizing the Servant of God’s spirit and action with precise and original details. The consistency of the facts, in different circumstances and different places, withstands all possible criticism and attests their authenticity and value.

Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi, who met her when she herself entered the house in Piacenza (August 1869), at once had the impression, which later became absolute certainty, of having come across an exceptional religious.

She wrote:

“I was edified by her humble and recollected bearing, by her manner full of gentleness and charity towards all and by her exact observance of her religious duties, and from then on I regarded her as a truly beautiful soul dear to the Lord.”

So far the praise, but the sister backs up this testimony with something very specific from her time with the Servant of God, when, some months after her clothing, she was assigned to her as a companion to nurse a poor sick woman:

“It was then,” the sister continues, “that I could admire her exquisite charity both towards the sick woman and towards me. We were allowed, if the patient was not so ill as to need both sisters at once, for one to rest on a chair until midnight while the other looked after the patient, and after midnight for the latter to rest while the other took over. Now Sister Anna del Salvatore wanted me to rest first and told me to rest easy, and that if my help was needed she would call me; and so as not to upset her I obeyed; but instead of sleeping I watched, without her noticing, how she cared for the poor patient, because, I repeat, I esteemed her greatly and wanted to see with how much love and charity she served the sick.”

And if this mention of the charity of her service were not enough, here is what else Sister Anna Elisabetta observed and recalled so precisely forty-four years later:

“This poor patient was all swollen, with dropsy I think, and her legs were covered in sores. Sister Anna del Salvatore, thinking I was asleep and could not see what she was doing, quietly unbandaged the poor woman’s ulcerated legs and dressed them, and then, what surprised and greatly edified me and confirmed me more and more in my belief in her holiness from those early years, I saw her lick the sores of that wretched woman with her tongue, kiss them tenderly and bandage them again with truly admirable charity.

I never said anything about what I had seen, because I was sure that, given her great humility and the care she took to hide her heroic virtues, she would have been upset to be discovered in so compassionate and heroic an act; but I could never forget it, and my veneration for her grew.”

Sister Anna Elisabetta, who said she was ready to swear to the truth of her testimony, adds that she never managed to make her rest, and that when her turn came she went on nursing until the next morning. These precise details fully justify what is said next, namely that “one could truly see that it was her delight to serve the sick, in whom she truly recognized the adorable person of Jesus, and she always preferred the poorest”.174

17. - In keeping with the customs of the time in the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Sister Anna del Salvatore too made her novitiate first in Piacenza and then in the houses where help was needed.

There was no lack of work, and it was awaited and sought by all as clergy and people came to know the Daughters of Saint Anne and appreciate their work of charity.

The Servant of God’s first place of formation and field of apostolate was Liguria, Mother Rosa Gattorno’s homeland. Unfortunately the Biographical Notes written soon after her death say little about these early activities, because, despite the abundance of reflections and praise, no doubt already deserved by Sister Anna del Salvatore, they remain rather general. Yet some concrete facts emerge, confirmed elsewhere and entirely credible, such as the joy she felt on receiving the religious habit; the forms of her constant commitment to obedience, service and sacrifice; her love of God expressed in caring for the suffering; and her constant spirit of prayer and penance, as seen in some other documented episodes.175

Although, as already mentioned, the testimonies known to us are few, they are compensated by their reliability. Sister Anna Paolina Viani, another sister, presents a series of facts that justify the biographer’s abundant praise.

Sister Anna Paolina, who lived with the Servant of God for some years in various houses, says that she admired at close quarters her heroic virtues and holiness of life, and therefore, out of duty of conscience, affection and veneration for her, felt able to testify to what she had observed “regarding her manner of life, exemplary in every way”:

“I first knew her between the end of 1871 and the beginning of 1872. I was in the house in Genoa (opened at that time) and she was in the house at Sampierdarena; as the places were close, it was easy to see each other. Even then the sisters spoke of the exemplary conduct of this good sister, though there was nothing singular about it. One admired in her great humility, obedience, charity towards all, and scrupulous exactness in fulfilling her duties and observing the Holy Rule; in short, she was a great edification.”176

For her part Sister Anna Guida confirmed the reputation her fellow sister enjoyed at that time and in those places, writing:

“When she was at Sampierdarena I learned that she worked hard at night: washing, carrying stones… I remember that once we wanted to give her a little party, I don’t remember whether for Christmas or some other occasion, and good Sister Salvatore, who disliked praise and celebrations, had hidden. It took a lot of effort to find her, and then, to make her attend the party, we had to catch her unawares somewhere. In fact she stood among the Sisters and girls, who were also standing, so absorbed that she seemed more in heaven than on earth.”177

Around 1872 Sister Anna del Salvatore was in Genoa with the other home-nursing sisters,178 and the recollections of her fellow sister Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi once again characterize the Servant of God’s response to her vocation in both contemplative and active life. Sister Anna Crocifissa’s testimony reads:

“What I can say of Sister Anna del Salvatore: Her prayer was continuous and fervent. Her charity towards the poor was very great; she cared for them lovingly and comforted them with words burning with the love of God.

Once in Genoa I went to do a night watch with Sister Anna Salvatore; I was very sleepy, and she said to me: sleep, I will do everything for the patient; and when there was nothing to be done for the patient I saw her several times on her knees praying; then, when the woman died and I was very frightened, she had me stand aside and went on praying.

When she saw God offended she would exclaim: O Paradise, O desert, so ardent was her desire to be united with God. At holy Mass and when she received Jesus in the Sacrament into her heart she was deeply recollected. She always came back from work cheerful, delighting everyone at recreation; the joy of her heart shone in her face, and she was always cheerful and serene.”179

From the start of her mission at Sampierdarena the Servant of God devoted all her energy to the success of the work. A group of letters from Don Antonio Accinelli to Mother Rosa tells us about the first steps in that house, which under her direction made steady progress.

“The house at Sampierdarena,” the priest wrote on 10 April 1873, “already has a confessor, Fr. Ferrari, director of the Pietrine sisters, an excellent person […]. The kitchen at Sampierdarena has been beautifully finished, and the absolutely necessary dormitory will soon be finished too. The roof has been repaired, so the water will stay out of the house. Salvatora [sic, for Sister Anna del Salvatore] manages well and is loved by all.”180

On 27 March 1873, as Holy Week approached, Don Accinelli expressed the wish “to be able to set up the Altar of Repose” and, on the following Thursday, to hold in the same church the Clothing ceremony of some Genoese postulants. He continues:

“Salvatora carries out the office of Superior very well. Today repair work began on the house to protect it from the water.”

Various benefactors, including the Foundress’s own father, helped to make the work easier and cheaper:

“Papa is seeing to it and it will not cost much,” writes Don Accinelli about the renovation of the house; “the kitchen range is being made entirely new with two Ronfé burners; Signor Baldi has had everything measured, and only half will be paid, the other half he is giving as a gift.”

The devout priest had not been mistaken in judging the virtues and good will of the Servant of God, and these letters of his are a recognition and an echo of the esteem and gratitude of the whole city, which benefited from the Daughters of Saint Anne and among them from Sister Anna del Salvatore, now ready for profession: she made her temporary profession on 26 July 1873, while her perpetual profession can be dated to 26 July 1881. It is true that Sister Anna del Salvatore’s name does not appear in the oldest register of professions, but this is because at that time the novitiate of the Daughters of Saint Anne lasted three years, the first of which, as mentioned, was spent in Piacenza and the other two in the various houses where the novices’ work was needed. At the end of the three years the novices took simple vows and renewed them annually with the Mother’s permission; but the local Superiors did not always send this information to the Mother House. This continued until the Rule was approved ad experimentum (1885).181

The Genoa community consisted of twelve (or thirteen) sisters, listed in the letter of 8 June: “At Sampierdarena, Superior Salvatora, Sisters Vernengo, Ludovica, Emanuella, Giacinta, Filomena, Addolorata, Angela, Ippolita, Chiara, Giulia, Bianca”, as well as two postulants who, by Mother Rosa’s order, were to go to Piacenza after their clothing:

“As for the postulants,” the devout priest continues, “I will do as you say: after the clothing I will send them to Piacenza; but we shall need to keep one here to help Sister Angela in the school and to teach the girls handwork, because the sisters we have are good nurses but not suited to handwork and teaching, and we need this badly here, as numbers keep growing; we now have 40 (pupils) and no more have been admitted without payment; the premises are becoming too small. I hear you have other houses to open; at this rate, in a few years the Daughters of Saint Anne will have occupied the whole peninsula and will be of great benefit to the Church, if they keep the spirit of their institution firm, of which I have no doubt.”182

In the light of these and other testimonies, we can appreciate even better the importance of a handful of letters written by the Servant of God from Sampierdarena to the Foundress and to a Superior of the Institute between 20 March and 6 July, shortly before she made her temporary vows.

In these letters Sister Anna del Salvatore reported on the running of the house and the daily events of the community, but above all on the spiritual life, as Mother Rosa had instructed her; with great humility the Servant of God showed that she shared the Mother’s trust in Providence and in Saint Anne’s heavenly protection.

These letters show the intimacy, always combined with great respect, and the trust Sister Anna del Salvatore had in the Foundress, to whom she spoke with moving spontaneity, as if writing to her own mother.

“Holy patience… I don’t know if you will understand me. Dear Mother, I am writing these few lines while keeping the night watch…” So begins the first letter, with an account of the alms collected and other news about the liturgy of the eve and feast of Saint Joseph, the exposition of the Blessed Sacrament and the care of the sick. Acts of submission, a request for forgiveness for a “mistake” and the fear of not having expressed herself clearly in another letter are followed by a firm resolution to be more careful and the admission that she is afraid of not making herself understood in writing. This too is an act of humility.183

The second letter was also written during a night watch and, like the previous one, bears as a heading the initials of the words: “Blessed be our glorious Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate”, and “May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us”.

The Superior to whom the letter is addressed had gone to Rome, and Sister Anna del Salvatore was sorry to have to be away from her for so long: “I hope the Lord will make your [journey] to Rome go well too, but I am sorry I don’t see you any more… I look for you everywhere, and I just don’t see you any more.” The sisters and boarders were sad too, but the Servant of God resigned herself to this absence and took on her responsibilities, which she would instinctively have avoided:

“For me it is like a continual martyrdom, my dear, patience… I am ready to do everything you told me. As long as my God is pleased, and my dear Mother, and you… and Mother Saint Anne. […] tell dear Mother that I am ready to do whatever she commands, and though I am incapable, God can do all things.”184

The third letter of that Ligurian period is again a request for Mother Rosa’s forgiveness for not having informed her about a sister, apparently concerning her health. Sister Anna del Salvatore had not written about it for fear of upsetting the Mother. She then spoke of internal matters of the house at Sampierdarena and repeated her act of humility, writing: “Mother, I am all in a muddle… I don’t know if you will have understood me, patience.” She asks “a blessing for herself and for all the dear Sisters”, and adds in a postscript: “I hope at least you have understood me.”185

Reporting on the community, and in particular on the health of the sisters and the boarders, the Servant of God asked for instructions about their sea bathing and confessed her fear of being unable to organize (it was already early July) the feast of Saint Anne and prepare the girls for Confirmation; she therefore begged the Mother to come and see to things in her place. Her words, which reveal such sincerity and virtue, deserve to be quoted:

“Dear Mother,” she writes, “what am I to do for Saint Anne, poor ignorant woman that I am, without education… Mother, think about it and you will see that it is true […]. Tell me how and to whom I should say it, and I will obey you in everything […]. Mother… do me this kindness… because Don Accinelli tells me that besides the Archbishop he is expecting many other priests and laypeople too; imagine, Mother, whether I am capable; my legs are starting to shake; believe me, Mother, it is really true.”186

A letter of 30 September from Don Accinelli to Mother Rosa, in a reference to the superior of the community (“the house at Sampierdarena is going fairly well; of the Superior I can say little so far, but she seems to me very behind with her accounts and not good at presenting herself”), suggests that Sister Anna del Salvatore was perhaps no longer with those sisters.187

Other documents show that around 1874 she was at Sestri Ponente, apparently for health reasons,188 while the other Ligurian house, where disorders had meanwhile occurred, was calling for her return.

After referring to the unfavorable circumstances reported by the sisters and verified by himself, the devout priest wrote on 8 November 1874:

“In short, a radical reform is needed in that house. It is true that the seed of discord will always remain, but with a prudent Superior at the head it can be stifled. Perhaps you have none available; Sister Salvatore with two good sisters around her will do. Let this be an example to you, Mother: do not trust youth; better a rough old woman than an educated young one; remember that when the Lord wished to punish a people he gave them a young king. Go slowly in accepting houses; consider whether you have someone to put in charge, otherwise you will see what happened at Sampierdarena happen elsewhere.”189

This is a clear recognition of the virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore, the only one considered available and, though still young, capable of restoring order in a community.

Meanwhile, however, the Servant of God had been transferred to Umbria.

18. - In May 1874 Mother Rosa, who had already opened a school in Foligno, went to San Martinello (San Martino ai Colli) to see the place where the Daughters of Saint Anne had been invited to open a school for poor children. The offer came from the Marchioness Edvige Spinola, on the advice of the Princess of Piombino, Donna Agnese Boncompagni Ludovisi, who already knew Mother Gattorno and appreciated her work. The house at San Martinello, furnished and funded by the Spinola family, was opened towards the end of November by Sister Anna Vincenza Rapallino, Sister Anna Eufemia Camporesi, its first superior, and other Daughters of Saint Anne.190 On 2 December Sister Anna Eufemia sent very encouraging news of the new foundation, writing enthusiastically:

“I have no words to describe how happy I am at San Martinello and how kind and attentive the Marchioness is. She is always thinking of us and is very fond of us, being so pleased with the schools, both for the number of pupils, of whom we already have more than two hundred, and for what they are taught; she is especially mad about the singing, and the Marquis goes everywhere praising them highly. Dear Mother, let us pray the Lord that we may continue to satisfy them.”191

Sister Anna del Salvatore certainly fulfilled these hopes with her virtues. Of this period, which was certainly very short, since by the autumn of 1875 she was already in Florence, we have a reliable testimony from Sister Anna Consolata Massimelli, Provincial Superior of Northern Italy, in a letter to the then Secretary General, Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega (30 November 1890). Sixteen years had passed since the two sisters had lived together at San Martinello, but the witness’s memory was still very clear. Besides, the distant impressions made on her by the Servant of God’s behavior and by the expression on her face were of the kind that, once felt, can never be forgotten. Nor were these generalities, afterthoughts or reinterpreted memories. What Sister Anna Consolata stated matches all the other testimonies from different times and places, but here she speaks of specific facts she herself observed, reported in the letter as follows:

“About our dear Saint I can tell you little, because she was very hidden.

It is saints who understand one another without speaking, not saints and sinners; but sinners admire the saints and envy them.

The first time I had the good fortune to meet Sister Anna del Salvatore was at San Martinello. Her presence struck me, she had so much of the angelic about her. She was very mortified, and seeing her so wasted, I cleverly made her eat the food the community provided, and she just as cleverly kept trying to mortify her appetite.

In the house at San Martinello she always woke me in the morning, and I always found the sister half-dressed, kneeling at a window opposite the Marchioness’s (Spinola) church, adoring Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament. I always pretended not to see her, so as to leave her to make love with the Lover of souls.”192

Concerning the time Sister Anna del Salvatore spent at San Martinello, Sister Anna Serafina Mazzinghi reports what she was told by an elderly sister, Anna Macrina Paolini, who knew “this Sister Anna del Salvatore, (who) was the cook in the house at San Martinello, a village of Perugia, and, considering this sister’s goodness, she seemed to her very mortified in everything”.193

It is not much, certainly, but it is still a further testimony to the work and virtue the Servant of God always practized, to the great edification of others.

19. - The proof of virtue and ability the Servant of God gave at San Martinello too, as in the other houses where she had been formed and had behaved as a true Daughter of Saint Anne, convinced Mother Rosa to entrust her with an even more demanding task.

The beginning of the work in the city of the Lily, until a few years earlier the capital of Italy, was not easy; indeed, although in June 1873 the Foundress, on her way back to Rome, had already agreed to open a house that August, it took a long time to obtain authorization from the diocesan authority. Only on 22 February 1875 could Mother Rosa write to Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega: “Yesterday it was settled that we go to Florence; this excellent Archbishop wants us there as nurses only.”194

The task of launching the new work had been entrusted to Sister Anna Benedetta, formerly the Marchioness Carrega, who through birth, family ties and friendships had excellent access to the best Florentine society. She naturally used it to make the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne known, and help was never again lacking, especially from Donna Luisa Strozzi, of whom a society columnist of the time wrote:

“Princess Strozzi, born Princess Centurioni of Genoa, lady-in-waiting to the Queen, is held to be strict, inflexible, an observer of the strictest rules of social etiquette […]. This does not, however, prevent her from having the kindest and most generous heart in the world. There is no charitable work in which her name does not shine first, and her palace, from the courtyard to the great hall, has often served as a splendid stage for the exploits of philanthropy.”195

Such, in secular language, was the understanding of charity, which in the case of that lady and many other outside collaborators of the Institute was inspired by a genuinely Gospel spirit.

The Florence work began around 1875, and on 27 February of that year Mother Rosa wrote to Sister Anna Benedetta, who was still in the house in Genoa:

“My Benedetta, for pity’s sake look after yourself, because the work now under way is immense. Soon Florence, and there will be plenty of work; what a lovely letter the Archbishop wrote me! I can’t wait to go. More postulants have come, and all good ones.”196

Later, in the letter of 8 July, the Mother again insisted, worried about the sister’s exertions: “I am always afraid you overtire yourself; mind, I order you to look after yourself.”197

On 18 November Mother Rosa announced the arrival of Sister Anna del Salvatore and gave Sister Anna Benedetta instructions about her work.

“For the moment,” she wrote, “it is best that you settle in, and Sister Anna del Salvatore can go out collecting alms, as she always did in Genoa too; then, once settled, you will be able to do better. (…) Tell Sister Anna del Salvatore to write to me and try to take on some nursing, and I will send her two good nurses at once; meanwhile see how things go, and I shall be guided by your letters. Courage, I hope this sister will do well, because she is good, very capable and has a true vocation.”198

When the Servant of God arrived at the house at Via Guelfa 103, Sister Anna Benedetta, her Florentine mission completed, received these orders:

“As soon as you receive this letter of mine from the sister, tell her everything you have done and then leave at once; don’t worry, this sister is very practical, because she has already set things up with me. So leave alone as soon as possible; I am expecting you. Pay the rent, and let the rest stay there for now.”199

The new superior at once faced serious difficulties, and on 27 November she described the situation to the Mother as anything but encouraging, so bad in fact that, without the comfort of faith and firm hope resting on the goodness of the cause, it could have been called desperate. For three days it poured with rain and the sisters did not even have an umbrella to go out of the rooms they occupied!200

Mother Rosa’s help solved this problem too, but the hardships were not over. Seeing the situation realiztically, still lacking the Archbishop’s permission to beg and with help from the Florentine ladies slow to come, Sister Anna del Salvatore did not despair. The whole community lived in a single room;201 some small help began to arrive (with the job of making five thousand tickets for a charity fair), and the sisters were nonetheless “good, cheerful and happy”. The Servant of God looked for sick people to nurse; she had found a confessor, who at once wanted to enroll her in the confraternity of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (but she replied that she had to ask the Mother’s consent), and with her spontaneity and simplicity she went on obeying the Mother, never hiding from her the difficulties they lived in. And she never stopped praying and working; indeed:

“In the cash box,” she wrote on 3 December, “there are still 96 lire… Believe me, dearest Mother, I do all I can not to spend, but what can I do? Until the Lord takes pity on this little family, I cannot put anything aside. Perhaps it is because I am not capable, or perhaps because I don’t do what I should, but be that as it may, I shall be ever more content, because it is better that he makes us feel something now rather than later: it means it is truly God’s will. And then, as long as I can please you, my dear Mother, I would be the happiest and most contented of all creatures.”202

Always eager to sacrifice herself for the good of others, the Servant of God wrote to the Mother regretting “with the greatest sorrow” that there were no sick to nurse; a Florentine prelate, Monsignor Giovannini, had reassured her that they would soon come, “that then there will be even too many, and we won’t know what to do”, and he himself “said that if he fell ill he wants the Daughters of Saint Anne”.203

Among the first people they nursed was a priest, and the Servant of God was happy to report to the Mother the words he kept repeating to his visitors: “Look what a lovely present Monsignor Archbishop gave me in sending me these dear Daughters. How happy I am!” Four sisters, including the Servant of God, took turns at night, and the patient seemed to be recovering.204

There would be no more lack of work. From then on the requests never stopped, and the Daughters of Saint Anne always accepted them; nursing the sick, and later educating girls, characterized the work they did in Florence in the spirit of the Institute: poverty, humility, anonymity, motherly devotion.

Without ever boasting of it, the Servant of God always saw to everything as well as possible, assisted by sisters who shared her spirit and her training.

As time went on and the correspondence with Mother Rosa grew, one notices that, while keeping her charming style, which we might call naïf, almost a shorthand record of her speech, Sister Anna del Salvatore had considerably improved her way of expressing herself, showing some cultural progress, not to speak of her spiritual progress, which went far beyond it.

The city responded to the sisters’ goodwill and ardent charity; the Archbishop encouraged them, and the benefactresses openly showed affection and admiration for the Daughters of Saint Anne and wanted them also for teaching Christian doctrine and running the home for the blind.205 The Mother approved this last project, championed by Princess Strozzi: “What luck, how happy I am,” wrote Sister Anna del Salvatore.206

This correspondence is full of expressions revealing the virtues and spirit of the Servant of God. She had not gone to meet the sisters at the station because she had one sister ill at home and two others out watching over other sick people; then, with another touch of her candor, she had not telegraphed the Mother as she had been asked, and excused herself:

“I was very afraid of making those telegraph clerks laugh with my blunders. Did I do wrong, Mother, to act like this? If I should do otherwise, I will.”207

20. - With the new year Sister Anna del Salvatore’s correspondence with the Foundress, whom she kept informed in detail of everything in the community, became more frequent. Between 2 January and 27 December 1876 at least the 42 letters208 preserved in the archive were sent from Florence to the Mother House, written by the Servant of God, whose grammar was improving while she kept the conversational and respectful style that would always characterize her writings.

Difficulties and consolations, obstacles and help alternated throughout this period. Sister Anna del Salvatore widened the field of charity and constantly showed good qualities in dealing with authorities and benefactors, in managing the Institute’s affairs and, as always, in helping the defenseless and unhappy people who turned to the Daughters of Saint Anne. The Servant of God’s peace of mind rested on her upright conscience, her prompt carrying out of the orders she received and her spontaneous, daily commitment to good works.

It is true that the ladies of the Florentine high aristocracy gave the Institute help and encouragement, but one also had to go along with their particular views as far as possible. Within these limits, and always with great respect and gratitude for the good received, Sister Anna del Salvatore held her peace and informed the Foundress:

“But what can you do, Mother,” she writes, “one needs a great deal of patience, well stored up, with these ladies! Well, let us not lose heart, for if Jesus wants to test us, he will reward us afterwards.”209

The difficulties seemed to ease, or at least, with the lodging settled and the circle of benefactors widened, Sister Anna del Salvatore no longer spoke of the hardships (which undoubtedly remained) but rejoiced instead in the exemplary conduct of her sisters:

“The sisters are well,” she wrote on 17 February. “They are really good, believe me, I am not telling lies; they keep silence so well that I often have to tell them they may speak once the time of strict silence is over; they are so obedient that I often have to tell them: let me finish what I am saying and then go; full of charity towards one another, prompt to get up in the morning and in all the rest of the day’s timetable.”210

Anna del Salvatore truly made herself “all things to all”: she saw to the new house to which the sisters would move211 and to vocations,212 which she examined with discernment, happy when they persevered but saddened when, for various reasons, the young women who had come forward could not enter the Institute.

A good girl, a postulant in Florence, was forced to leave the Institute because of her relatives’ threats. The poor young woman, having to give in, begged Sister Anna del Salvatore to be readmitted once the circumstances that obliged her to return to her family had ceased. The rule was inflexible on this point, but the Servant of God nevertheless tried to intercede for this favor.

“Dear Mother,” she wrote on 14 June 1876, “I have to give you this sorrow: that postulant from Peccioli, on the day I received your letter, her relatives came to take her away, and the reason is that her mother fell ill from grief and is at death’s door, and so wants her daughter at all costs. I did my best not to let her go, but they answered that wherever she might be, and whatever the cost, they wanted their daughter.

Ah, dear Mother, imagine how sorry I was… Believe me, I urged her not to go, but it was impossible… The poor girl was crying and begging me to take her back, saying she would plead with her mother and all her relatives to let her return, and I told her that if she goes home she will not be accepted again. But what can I do, Mother, the brother-in-law told me he would not leave without the girl; the girl, weeping bitterly, begged me for charity’s sake to ask the Mother to take her back; I said no. But do as you think best, Mother. She left her trunk and dowry; if you accept her, well and good; if not, I will send them to her.”213

She still had some hope, though, since not returning the departing postulant’s belongings may have concealed the wish that the Mother would soften the rules on readmitting those who left the community.

Yet even in her simplicity Sister Anna del Salvatore knew how to distinguish the merits and faults of those she had to report on, and to give the Mother what she needed to decide whether they should stay in the Institute. In the case of a postulant whom they had vainly tried to tame, the Servant of God wrote to Mother Rosa: “This morning (30 August) I called her, but I cannot persuade her; believe me, Mother, I have done all I am capable of. But it will be very difficult to succeed.” The obstacles were laziness, gluttony and poor adaptation to community life, already tried once before.

“Then she tells me,” the letter continues, “that in the convent where she was before, she stayed five years and liked it there, because each one kept what she liked in her chest of drawers…; that is, sweets, vin santo, rosolio and pastries, etc., etc. So, dear Mother, you can judge whether she can last among the Daughters of Saint Anne, or whether she has a vocation.”

Although she saw the matter clearly, Sister Anna del Salvatore once again deferred to Mother Rosa’s decision: “You tell me, dear Mother, what I should do.”214

In a few months in Florence the Servant of God had become well known to the clergy and the benefactresses and had learned to govern her community with discernment. She handled affairs very prudently, especially when it came to accepting people and starting new works; she also went out collecting alms in person in the city and the Tuscan provinces,215 happy whenever she could give the Mother encouraging news. Once she wrote: “the sisters are all well […], and such peace reigns among the good sisters that it is truly a pleasure.”216 But would that happy state last long?

Then came disappointments, and Sister Anna del Salvatore humbled herself, taking the blame when someone took advantage of her good faith and deceived her, to the Institute’s harm.

“How I have been deceived,” she wrote to Mother Rosa, “I never thought a creature could deceive like that; how sorry I am! I assure you, Mother, I will never do such a thing again. Ah, dear Mother, I beg you to forgive me; I do not deserve forgiveness, that is true, but in your goodness you will not be angry with me, though I deserve never to receive another letter from you. My heart is pierced for having caused you this trouble. I promise I will not do it again.”217

Sister Anna del Salvatore, always trusting in divine Providence, did not hide the difficulties, and when she could not personally meet the house’s constant needs she asked the Mother for help, with her usual humility and submission.

Giving good news of the nursery school, now attended by forty-five little girls, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote on 27 October: “if you think fit, we would need another sister so as to do everything better.”218 Three months earlier the nursery had only twenty-two or twenty-four pupils, while other planned initiatives, such as “supervising many boys and girls in a large factory outside Florence”, depended on a favorable answer from the Daughters of Saint Anne; otherwise nothing would be done.219

The reputation of the work and of the one directing it grew rapidly. A paragraph of the letter of 4 June seems to me very significant: the Servant of God lets slip a reference to her own activity in Florence but immediately corrects herself and attributes the merit to the whole community. The passage reads:

“As for alms, if it goes on like this it’s not bad, because almost every day, especially now that they are beginning to know me, I mean us, [we receive] four, five and some days even six francs.”220

But the happiest moment for Sister Anna del Salvatore was when she learned that her sister Veronica had been accepted among the Daughters of Saint Anne, and she wrote jubilantly to Mother Rosa:

“My Mother, what good fortune! What a grace, what consolation I feel on hearing that you have accepted my sister. Oh, how generously the Lord will reward you for such great charity… ah, believe me, Mother, I will be grateful to you all my life for so great a gift… Mother, after God you alone possess my life, my will, in short all of me as yours.”221

Besides looking after the Florence house, Sister Anna del Salvatore was asked to contact a lady in Pisa who wished to donate her house to the Institute, a house still held jointly with her sisters, which had given rise to complications. Moreover, the benefactress wanted only two sisters to go to that house (“which is very beautiful, [with] a lovely little chapel, and there is also a beautiful garden”), while the Servant of God replied: “it cannot be fewer than three.”

The parish priest, the letter of 23 June 1876 to the Mother continues, wished to send several postulants to the Institute, among them a niece of his, “a fine soul, good for work”, and would himself pay the dowry.222

Sister Anna del Salvatore showed these intentions by sparing no effort, even taking on the considerable task of writing for those who had learned as she had but were not yet skilled enough at it. On 23 February 1876 she told the Mother of the difficult situation of her sisters and pupils:

“The sisters who came from Piacenza,” writes the Servant of God, “can neither read nor write, especially one of them; the other knows her words well and is also beginning to read a little, so if you permit, I will teach her a little twice a week.”223

In a short time, under Sister Anna del Salvatore’s guidance, the Florence house got under way, and it even seemed that progress would not stop at the good results achieved but would bear further good fruit.

“Mother Gattorno,” writes her first biographer, “answered each of her letters, encouraging her to think that God would take account of her work, for which one day she would be worthily rewarded, praising her for what she did and lovingly and wisely advising her to persevere in doing good. And the grateful, affectionate daughter kissed that letter again and again like something sacred, laughing and crying at once for joy; fired by the sense of her duty and the promise of the reward she would earn by fulfilling it, she found her cross too light compared with the happiness she could later attain by bearing it with resignation, and prayed the Lord to make it heavier by adding new tribulations.”224

But her relationship with the Mother in those years was not only by letter; on her journeys to Rome Blessed Rosa stopped in Florence, which had by now become one of the main centers of activity of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Under Sister Anna del Salvatore’s government the girls’ school was founded and flourished in “a very beautiful house” at Via Faenza 54; the Mother visited it in November 1876 and found it running excellently. Besides the school curriculum the boarders learned French and music. The Servant of God and the other sisters divided their time between the Institute’s two characteristic works: home nursing and the education of girls. A visit from Sister Anna Benedetta (October 1877) to start the new school year in the spirit and according to the guidelines of the Foundress was also a great comfort to the Servant of God.225

21. - Florence, though not very generous to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, nonetheless showed its gratitude in practical ways for a work that met so many of the population’s needs. The Servant of God always expressed her gratitude, even for small gifts and promises made to her, and informed the Mother accordingly, as can be seen in this letter (and many others):

“Yesterday the Marchioness Covoni came to see me and brought me the medicine, and […] then she asked how many of us there are; I told her we were 17, and then she asked if we have debts; I said no, but that for several days we had had no peace because of the rent of the house, and she told me that if that was the cause of my worry I could rest easy, she would see to it, as long as I was at peace. I don’t know if I did wrong, but I did it on purpose to see whether she would pay the rent for me, as I hoped.”

The number of sick to be nursed grew so fast that, as Sister Anna del Salvatore writes, “if it goes on like this, 20 or even 30 sisters will not be enough”.226

As already mentioned, apart from another letter thanking the Mother for sending Sister Anna Fabiana to Florence227 and later a request to pass on to her mother, who was really in need, some alms intended for the poor, the Servant of God makes no other reference to her family, except concerning her brother’s illness, which sadly proved fatal.

The Servant of God had asked the Mother by telegram for permission to go to the bedside of her dying brother, who ardently wished to see her before closing his eyes for ever.

The answer was no, and the Servant of God, far from resenting it, accused herself to the Mother of having made the request. As if it had been inappropriate, she asked forgiveness and humbled herself to the point of signing the letter “ungrateful and unworthy daughter”.

The document, entirely in the Servant of God’s own hand, reads:

“A few hurried lines because it is late,” she writes on 18 January 1877. “Mother, I beg you for charity’s sake to forgive my boldness, because at that moment I did not know what I was doing. Oh, how sorry I am to have telegraphed you! But what can I say, at that moment I let myself be carried away by love for my brother. But I assure you I will not let myself be carried away again; yet what could I do, when a telegram came telling me my brother was dying and wanted to see me one last time to say a word to me, and that after speaking to me and seeing me he would die happy and at peace… Then I learned from my sister that she too, before leaving home, when he was already ill, saw him all pale and he asked for me; and my sister asked him what he wanted, and he said: Ah! if only I could see Sister Anna del Salvatore!… Poor boy, how good he was; he is 20 or 21, perhaps he has died. Tell me, dear Mother, what will become of that soul!”228

After what the community needed had been set aside, the alms with which the townspeople rewarded the Daughters of Saint Anne for their labors were sent to Piacenza; and since the Mother was surprised at these offerings, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote to her:

“Dear beloved Mother. I have received your dear letter, in which I see you were surprised at the money I sent you. Dear Mummy, if I may call you so, you know well it is a duty to help you where we can, and besides it was yours. So I have done nothing. Would to God I could give you what I wish!”229

At other times the Servant of God accused herself of incompetence in drawing up the house accounts, while the other sisters, who had more education, sent Mother Rosa impeccable financial reports.
