She likewise apologized for the results that emerged and promised to redo everything to show exactly how much had come in and how much gone out.

Always with her natural spontaneity and above all her deep humility, the Servant of God wrote to the Foundress:

“My dear beloved Mother. All your dear daughters will send you their accounts in perfect order; only poor Sister Anna del Salvatore does not know how to do it, and perhaps not even you, my good dear Mother, will be able to understand, poor thing, how she will manage. I beg you to be patient, because my ability goes no further. Ah, I assure you, dear Mother, it is a great sorrow to me not to be able to make myself understood, and I am even sorrier for the trouble you will have looking at those accounts, which you certainly won’t be able to understand, because I can’t understand them either; well, I want to hope the Holy Spirit will make you understand them…” And in the postscript: “Dear Mother, I am sorry because I find such a discrepancy in the accounts, that is, I find more expenditure than income. I will go over the books again scrupulously and then send you the result again.”230

A few months later, candidly confessing her boundless trust in Providence, she added:

“Dear Mother […] please do not worry… Jesus will provide, because he is my treasurer, so I don’t think about anything, because Jesus sees I am a stubborn little donkey, and so he thinks of everything. Yesterday the bread bill came (and) I burst out laughing because I had only 30 francs and the bill was almost 90, but the Lord, so good, provided me with that and more besides… So I am happy, because I don’t think about anything.”231

Then, when things looked promising financially too, thanks to the promises of a supposed benefactress staying in the Florence house, who kept saying she would buy a house for the Institute at her own expense, a serious disappointment came: she went back on her word.232 Sister Anna del Salvatore informed the Foundress at once:

“As for the 2000 francs, she keeps promising them to me, but I have good reason to believe she will not give them any more, because yesterday,” she writes on 3 May, “she told me so many lies that I would never have believed a soul could lie so much; so whoever says one thing and then unsays it does not deserve to be believed.”

And the needs kept growing: “We have so many sick people that I really don’t know what to do, and almost all recommended by benefactors: I am in a real muddle.” So she wrote in the same letter in which she asked advice and permission to receive a postulant.233

Otherwise life went on at its usual pace, and only once, as far as the documents we have show, did Sister Anna del Salvatore have to take severe measures, against her will, with a sister. She apologized for it to the Mother, to whom the postulants sent to Piacenza would already have reported the matter. The Servant of God had punished the sister by keeping her at home and not sending her out to collect alms,

“and this is the heaviest penance,” she writes to Mother Rosa, “especially for that one […]. Now all is calm.”

It seems other Sisters had also been at fault in some way, for the letter continues:

“I am afraid I did wrong because I scolded them severely, and now things are quite different; today they had a lovely recreation, it was a pleasure to see them; they promised me it will not be as it was for 7 or 8 days in a row.”234

As we read in the recent profile of Sister Anna del Salvatore,235 during her time in Florence there were some extraordinary episodes reminiscent of the Fioretti.

There is the story of a girl in the boarding school who, after the death of her benefactor and only support, no longer had the means to pay her fees and studies and tried to take her own life by drinking a potion in which the contents of a whole box of matches had been dissolved. The situation seemed hopeless; the doctor, called at once together with a priest, judged that nothing could be done, but as soon as Sister Anna del Salvatore was told, though she was confined to bed with a high fever, she rushed to the unhappy girl and knelt before the Crucifix praying for her life. Shortly afterwards, without the doctor being able to do anything, the girl vomited the poison and was saved.

The other fioretto dates from 1876, when a large debt had built up, there were only a few coins in the cash box, and no fewer than twenty-two people to feed. Sister Anna del Salvatore was not alarmed; she went out with another sister to Santa Maria Novella, where she became absorbed in fervent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament.

A lady interrupted her prayer and handed the sister an envelope, insisting that she accept it. The stranger refused to give her name and left the church. The two sisters tried to follow her to see where she lived so as to thank her, but she had vanished. When the heavy envelope was opened, it contained the exact sum the Daughters of Saint Anne owed the baker to settle their arrears.

The novice Anna Anastasia Cecconi had been assigned as Sister Anna del Salvatore’s companion; at that time she suffered from a disease of the lymph glands, so Fr. Andreotti, a Piarist who gave spiritual assistance to the community, insisted on sending her home to be treated better. Convinced it would be for a short time, the young woman laid aside her habit and went back to her family, but soon realized not only that the treatment would be long, but that her return home had been a trick of Andreotti’s to prevent her from coming back to the Institute, since the Foundress’s permission was conditional on a quick recovery.

“A few days later the distressed Cecconi,” writes Sister Anna Roberta, “returns to Florence to her superior and begs her to keep her, because she wants to be faithful to her vocation. Sister Anna del Salvatore welcomes her like a mother and undertakes to clarify her situation with Mother Rosa Gattorno. The rigidity of the times would not allow her to take her in, but she considers that charity comes before everything, and suffers much opposition for it. The Foundress finally understands that Fr. Andreotti’s harshness is unjustified, and Sister Anna Anastasia is readmitted to community life.”

The Daughters of Saint Anne remembered Cecconi as an excellent religious who held positions of responsibility, and they also handed down the words with which she referred to those events: “I owe my religious life to Sister Anna del Salvatore.”236

The source of this information is the report Sister Anna Letizia Sordi sent from Appignano on 21 November 1890 to Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega:

“Now I shall pass to something else,” writes Sister Anna Letizia, after giving news of the house, the nursing and the school. “Since you have asked me to tell you what I know of Sister Anna del Salvatore, I do so very willingly. I shall say what I remember without choosing my words, just as I saw it with my own eyes, heard it with my own ears, held it in my own hands, in the presence of God, without fear of saying a word that is not true. During 1877, when she was superior in Florence, on many nights after midnight or one o’clock I got up to go and see where she was. Almost always I found her kneeling on the floor, leaning on a chair, burning with love and shedding abundant tears before the Tabernacle. I begged her to go to bed, but she did not realize it was so late and (said) she had to keep Jesus company, as he was all, all alone. In the morning after Holy Communion she hid her face in her hands, and one could shake her or call her: all in vain.

[…] In any circumstance, whatever grace she wished to obtain, or if the Mother commended some need to her, she immediately turned to the prayer of the Filotea, ‘Here I am before you, O great Queen of heaven, etc.’, and obtained what she asked; the next day she would tell the sisters: ‘The Mother, or such a person, has received the grace.’ In her conversations she always spoke of Jesus’ love for us, of Magdalen pushing her way among the soldiers accompanying Jesus to Calvary, and how he looked at her and called her by name. She always spoke of Jesus as a fisherman, and when she saw fish she would say: Ah, how I would like to catch big fish for Jesus. She would always exclaim: From the tabernacle a voice constantly comes, telling us to love Jesus.

[…] In winter, in the bitter cold, she was found wearing only her black habit and black bodice. Her stockings were always torn, with her feet showing, her shoes broken; and if one wanted to upset her so much as to make her cry, it was enough to make her something new. There was no way of making her wear it. She gave it to another sister. As for food, she ate only once every 24 hours. Sometimes I forced her to take a little piece of chocolate in the morning. After much suffering she would bring it up. She always ate pulses and food that had gone bad for several days and said it was delicious... because, she said (out of humility), I have always been a little beast, a little animal.

She almost always wore a hair shirt made like a net, with points close together on the inside; it was of iron but shone like steel from constant use. However much she hid it, we noticed that she suffered a great deal when getting up and sitting down. On Fridays she never left it off, to this I can testify. She had several, a shorter one to wear on the thighs. She had even allowed me to wear this one during the hours of strict silence, something I could not keep up for long.

In Florence in 1877 she had a phlegmon on her arm. The sisters insisted on calling the doctor. Before he came in, the Superior begged and implored them to leave her alone for a moment. They did not, because they suspected she wanted to take off her hair shirt. And so it was: before the doctor arrived the hair shirt fell to the floor and was picked up by a sister, to her great distress.

I have experienced the power of her prayers. Some years ago I suffered terrible temptations against Holy Purity. I wrote to the Mother, who told me to make a novena to Sister Anna Salvatore, that true saint, and my prayer was answered. That is all I can tell you, frankly and sincerely, as I would say it if I had to die this very moment.”237

These and other first-hand testimonies are very significant as regards the Servant of God’s practice of the virtues, among which charity stood out. Marianna Orsi’s whole life is marked by acts and conduct that fully reflect her spiritual life and the degree she reached in it.

But if virtue was the constant mark of the Servant of God in ordinary circumstances, it would shine especially in the days of painful trial that were now approaching. Although she faced them with great faith in divine justice, even before her innocence was recognized it must have been especially painful for Sister Anna del Salvatore, so attached to the Institute and its rules, to be accused of things she had never done, so much so that the slanders spread against her had adverse repercussions even within the Institute, though for a relatively short time.

22. - Around the middle of 1877 a storm gathered over Sister Anna del Salvatore’s head. Although she had noticed the signs, she went on serenely praying and working for the glory of God and the salvation of souls, while continuing to accuse herself of faults which in her humility seemed real to her but which she had never committed. This attitude made her an easy target for ill-disposed men. Accusing herself of incompetence in facing the difficulties that beset her, the Servant of God begged for the Mother’s presence, but the Mother had had to postpone her visit to Florence, an obligatory stop on her journeys to Rome. Deeply grieved, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote to her:

“What sorrow, what pain I feel! I am wicked, it is true, yes, but to the point of being deprived of your presence, that I never, never thought. Ah, dear Mother, I beg you for charity’s sake to come by here, not for me but for the good of the house and of the whole Institute.”

At that time there was the question of buying a house, which Fr. Andreotti of the Piarists was handling; having good connections in Florence, he had recommended the matter to several gentlemen, to his Provincial Celestino Zini and especially “to that famous religious Fr. Ricci”, as the letter of 20 May 1877 continues. The opportunity to buy the house was such that, she adds, “if you let it go […] there might be no time left”.238

Relations with the Florentine clergy, however, were deteriorating. Following a request from Fr. Andreotti, which the Servant of God promptly granted, Don Niccolai, the community’s confessor, who had not been consulted (and was not entitled to be), vented all his resentment on Sister Anna del Salvatore and, refusing to listen to reason, gave up his office in the community.

In the letter of 24 May the Servant of God calmly gave her version of events, writing to the Foundress:

“Dear Mother, I have made a mistake, and it is this: the little girls made their first Communion on 3 May, and I thought that once they had been admitted to first Communion that was enough for always; so the next day Fr. Andreotti, who comes every morning to say Mass for us, told me, indeed begged me, to have them receive Communion for a benefactor, and he would prepare them with a short exhortation; and not thinking I was doing wrong, I agreed; I did go in the morning to see if I could find [Don Niccolai] to ask him, but I didn’t find him; and Fr. Andreotti also told me that once they have made it the first time, that is enough, and they can make it a second and third time whenever they wish; indeed he begged me, because he saw the girls so well disposed and well prepared… Ah, I wish I had never done it, because Niccolai scolded me severely and then wrote that he would not come any more… because I do everything without asking his opinion, and also because I put the confessional in the church…”

Finally she added:

“Don’t worry, dear Mother, perhaps it is better for us, because I know for certain he was entirely against us.”239

Meanwhile the rumors circulating in Florence against the Servant of God and her government increased. First of all, Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, vicar for religious and a confidant of the Archbishop, had been annoyed because Sister Anna del Salvatore had refused to agree (nor could she have) to the confessor’s request to turn the community into an enclosed monastery. These clashes with the secular clergy were made sharper by the preference given to Regulars, namely the Piarists, and one of them, Andreotti, whom the vicar for religious wanted removed from the care of the convent, as he later succeeded in doing. The Provincial was summoned for this purpose, and the Vicar had already sent him a letter on the subject. Fr. Zini behaved diplomatically, telling Monsignor Ciaranfi that he had “never been pleased with the interest the said Religious takes in those Sisters, for whom […] he has obtained good alms” and secured from the City Council some work on the house. Ciaranfi’s mistrust, or rather his jealousy at seeing how much the Piarists cared for and favored the Daughters of Saint Anne, grew when Fr. Mauro Ricci undertook “to write and print the devotions for the month of Saint Anne for the sisters’ use”, and on hearing, though this is not otherwise documented, that they had asked “to place themselves under the guardianship and protection of Saint Joseph Calasanz”. From what was said he had, in short, “seemed to see that behind Fr. Andreotti was Fr. Zini”.

Again to Archbishop Cecconi, Monsignor Ciaranfi complained that Sister Anna del Salvatore had not come back to consult him about certain priests, namely Don Niccolai, who had withdrawn, Don Ciolli, then confessor of the girls, and Don Fini, confessor of the sisters.240

A few days later, writing again to Monsignor Cecconi, Canon Ciaranfi reported that Fr. Andreotti had been to see him and had said he was ready to withdraw if the Archbishop wished.

“The Superior also came,” the letter continues, “with great shows of submission, asking my forgiveness a thousand times for any mistakes she may have made so far through not knowing the customs and practices of our Diogese (sic). She complained about Niccolai, who wanted to give orders outside the confessional too and was trying to get some young sisters to leave the Institute, promising to place them elsewhere. As for Fini [who had become the community’s confessor, though Don Ciolli had been appointed to it ad interim], she says that Signor Ciolli refused to hear the girls’ confessions, and she thought that, since they were laypeople, she could have them confess to whomever she wished. She promised never to do anything without consulting me, and in future to depend on me even in the smallest things; and so she showered me with compliments and expressions of great satisfaction at having been able to speak to me.”

The Vicar General had authorized Don Fini to hear the laywomen’s confessions until a permanent confessor was found, and for this office Ciaranfi proposed Don Lazzaro Lazzeri, who was anything but favorable to the sisters of Saint Anne.

There remained the mistrust, unjustified in our view, of Sister Anna del Salvatore, whom Ciaranfi (while passing on to the Archbishop her respects and her request for a blessing for herself and her sisters) did not fail to judge most unkindly, writing:

“The said Superior struck me as very shrewd, and I did not put much faith in her humble manners.”241

Ever more clearly hostile to the Servant of God and her community, the Vicar for religious specified that Don Lazzeri had accepted the office “solely out of obedience” to the Archbishop,

“as he is not well disposed towards the said Sisters; he would therefore like to be given a clear position, to avoid disputes and embarrassment. To this end I have drafted the letter to the Superior in clear terms and send it to Your Excellency, that you may kindly examine it and also sign it if you see fit.”242

The choice of a confessor so ill-disposed towards the Daughters of Saint Anne, and Monsignor Ciaranfi’s behavior towards the Servant of God, give a fairly clear idea of how much the situation was deteriorating.

Accused of insubordination, the Servant of God had seen her position improve somewhat thanks to the Mother’s visit to Florence. But it was only for a moment, as the accusations soon began to circulate insistently again.243 Fr. Andreotti’s visits to the house were restricted, and, far more serious, an anonymous letter full of vulgarity, insults and slanders against her honor as a woman and her consecration as a bride of the Lord outrageously wounded Sister Anna del Salvatore.

The defamatory libel certainly deserved no credence, but an echo of the priests’ mistrust of the work and its superior reached Piacenza and aroused in the Mother a suspicion that surfaced again in her correspondence with Sister Anna del Salvatore. With what anguish one can imagine, she wrote on 9 July to her “dear beloved Mother”:

“As great as my joy was on receiving your longed-for letter, so painful was it to read. O God, what sorrow, what great pain it was for me to hear that in this community [that is, Florence] there is so much disorder on my account. My God, what heartbreak… Ah, my dear Mother, if this happens through my fault, you who are so good can remove me so that I give no more scandal, and then this holy community will flourish and spread its beautiful branches through this lovely city; but I am ready to do in everything whatever you command, and if I had to stay in this community all my life I would do so willingly, as long as my dear Mother is pleased.”

The charge she answered was that she did not take part in “community exercises”, though only in the evening and midday prayers, not in the meditation and the Rosary. And she adds: “but I may be mistaken, because if you say so it must be true.”244

This act of sincere and genuine humility was probably taken for hypocrisy, and the accusation, thus aggravated, was believed for some time. In the summer of 1877 Fr. Andreotti’s position seemed to be clarified, though his visits to the house were reduced. He was also ordered that his conversations with the Sisters must always take place in the Superior’s presence.

At the end of August the Provincial of the Piarists laid down the conditions for the work Andreotti would do in the house of the Daughters of Saint Anne, namely preparing some sisters for the teacher-qualification examination.

First, the matter was recognized as

“necessary or at least very useful, and therefore approved by the ecclesiastical Curia, on whose jurisdiction,” writes Fr. Zini, “I must believe that the devout Society of the Sisters of Saint Anne acknowledges that it depends.”

The Piarist’s presence was not to be too frequent or too prolonged; therefore, says the third paragraph,

“with frequency and length of stay reduced to the bare minimum, there must be, in the judgment of the ecclesiastical Curia, moral certainty that the matter will escape comment from the public, always quick to think ill, and give no pretext for gossip and slander damaging the good name, not so much of individuals as of the two Institutes… As Fr. Andreotti would have to speak with the diploma candidates, such conversations were to take place in the presence of the Superior or her deputy, chosen from among the senior sisters. The permission, revocable by the Provincial without his having to give reasons ‘either to Fr. Andreotti or to anyone else’, thus limited the commitment to the sisters’ academic preparation only. The Archbishop’s rescript, at the Superior’s request, authorized the religious to go to the Institute no more than once a day and forbade any interference with the sisters themselves, in whose government and direction no mission can be admitted that is not recognized and approved by the diocesan Ordinary.”245

Yet, still accusing herself (“The sisters are all well and all good, truly little angels… Only I, the wretched one… But I hope to be converted by so many good examples of holiness”),246 Sister Anna del Salvatore went on governing the community, attending to the smallest matters and keeping the Mother informed; for Christmas 1877 she wrote:

“Dear Mother, you will say I never write to you, but I am so busy that I really can’t; by day I have to go out, and at night I am tired, so I have to fail in a strict duty of mine! But you are so good, I hope you will forgive me, won’t you?”247

In the letter of 21 February 1878, too, Sister Anna del Salvatore, against whom, as we have seen, Canon Ciaranfi’s misunderstanding and hostility were beginning to be directed, wrote to the Mother as if foreseeing what was about to happen to her:

“Dear Mother, I may have been wrong, but with you, my beloved Mother, I have always come with the plain truth… And besides, you are my mother, and rather than betray you or be unfaithful to you I would gladly suffer a thousand martyrdoms… Oh yes, I assure you that even if you sent me out of your holy Institute I would love you just the same and be faithful to you; but rejoice, Mother, for if Jesus permits these things it is because he wants you ever holier, and to make me atone for my many sins, which outnumber the stars of heaven! Oh dear Mother, I will pray Jesus hard that you may know me through and through, even the most secret thoughts of my heart!”248

Distressed less by the accusations against her than by the fear that Mother Rosa might believe them, Sister Anna del Salvatore begged to be relieved of her office:

“Dear Mother… to my great sorrow I hear again that I am not sincere. My God, what pain, what grief I feel!… Remove me, yes, I beg you for charity’s sake,” she had already written on 14 January, “because then I will stop causing you sorrow… I ask forgiveness for every mistake, but I am ready to do your will and not mine.”249

The disorders that came to light, with which Sister Anna del Salvatore had nothing whatever to do, must nonetheless have damaged her person and position. The accusations were made by a rebellious postulant who had already behaved in the same way elsewhere, in another Institute.250

As could easily have been foreseen, Don Lazzeri felt uncomfortable and, already prejudiced against the Daughters of Saint Anne, now no longer wanted to hear their confessions and insisted on resigning, according to Canon Ciaranfi’s report to the Archbishop, saying he “could not in conscience continue to exercise his ministry among them”. Even Monsignor Giovannini, Prior of San Lorenzo, who on the contrary had always been well disposed towards the Servant of God and her religious family, according to Ciaranfi now turned against them, “showing himself dissatisfied with them, and especially with the local superior, false and lying”, and saying further “that he did not see clearly in their conduct, and feared some comment that might compromise the said priest who puts up with them”. So Ciaranfi adds: “he asks that a remedy be found by requiring them either to submit to the direction given them by the diocesan Ordinary or to leave.” He concludes that, since both Monsignor Cecconi and Mother Rosa were in Rome, and since he had said this would be the Archbishop’s mind, the Monsignor Vicar too would like “to know something about it so as then to act accordingly”.251

But some ten days later Don Lazzeri changed his mind: he no longer intended to give up the office of confessor; “indeed he wishes to stay,” writes Ciaranfi, “because he hopes for good results from the superiors’ action.”252

23. - Between the end of January and early February 1878 the Servant of God had a few quiet days. She had been to Rome at the Mother’s wish, and now, traveling again, she went to Bologna to accompany some Florentine postulants who were then to go on to the house in Piacenza. Still carrying out her orders, Sister Anna del Salvatore set off again after completing this task and went to Osimo and Appignano. During the long train journey a gentleman (whose name is not given) asked her about the Institute, its activities and aims, and promised a large sum of money, as he said he had done for Don Bosco. We know nothing more, except that on reaching Osimo the Servant of God was received by the Bishop, who kept her and another sister to lunch. The Bishop too wanted to know about the Institute and asked whether the Mother would accept two postulants without a dowry.

As we learn from the letter she later wrote to the Mother, Sister Anna del Salvatore went on to Appignano, where she visited the parish priest and the mayor, then passed through Loreto to venerate Our Lady in the Holy House, and returned to Florence.253

The situation grew ever more serious. Left alone to fight for the survival and honor of the Institute in Florence, Sister Anna del Salvatore could not even defend herself, so far had her opponents won over the Vicar for religious and other priests, worthy men in themselves, swayed by negative inferences and insinuations about the Servant of God’s conduct.

The slanders had easily reached the Foundress’s ears, and she, who knew well Sister Anna del Salvatore’s spirit of obedience and absolute sincerity, ordered her to tell her “the plain truth”, which the Servant of God would in any case have told her even without a formal command, as she had always scrupulously done.

Having humbled herself so far as to take all the blame, or rather what she considered blame, the Servant of God nevertheless tried to defend herself against the attack of the Vicar for religious, who told her: “I tell you to stop telling lies.”

But what was it about? The sister herself explains in the letter to the Foundress already mentioned:

“Dear Mother, here are the words Ciaranfi said to me,” she writes on 21 February 1878: “I tell you to stop telling lies… And because I told Fr. Andreotti that it is not true that I told Ciaranfi he no longer needs to teach, and because I never go to see him, though he has told me many times to go on Wednesdays; and it is indeed true that he told me so when I went to give him the season’s greetings; I say it is true because I asked Sister Anna Giuseppina whether she remembered it, and she said yes.”254

The Mother then turned to the Vicar for religious, who eight days later wrote to the Archbishop:

“Sister Gattorno wrote to me warmly commending her sisters to me; I replied at once that I had been ordered by Your Excellency to take special care of them and would do so as best I could, trusting in their docility and cooperation.”

But here is how he exercised this care:

“The Superior here came to see me,” Ciaranfi continues, “and I tried politely to give her some general advice, and then promised I would visit the Institute. At this news she jumped for joy and, in a comic, overexcited way, showered me with thanks and praise. We shall see!”255

This shows clearly how willing the Vicar for religious was, and how willing the Servant of God was, to clear up the situation by establishing the truth. Sister Anna del Salvatore’s naive expressions of joy, gratitude and deference are interpreted as rather comic. And if only Monsignor Ciaranfi had stopped there! He saw in the Servant of God’s behavior a falseness that finds no support whatever in her conduct. If anything, it was Sister Anna del Salvatore who noticed Fr. Andreotti’s contradictions, as she goes on to say in the letter of 3 March 1878:

“Dear Mother, I beg you for charity’s sake to tell me how I should behave about collecting alms, because I don’t know what to do, since Fr. Andreotti tells me one thing one day and another the next, so I don’t know what to do… I can do little, because I am glad, and it is my duty, to try to be at home now to look after Signor Alessandro (…), and I haven’t the heart to let him eat without my being there.”256

Even her attentions to Mother Rosa’s son, Alessandro Custo, would be turned into a charge against Sister Anna del Salvatore, though the arrows were aimed at the Mother and the Congregation, regarded as intruders, forgetting all the hidden and visible good that the Daughters of Saint Anne had done in Florence in those years under the Servant of God’s guidance and were still doing.

Meanwhile a new development filled Sister Anna del Salvatore with dismay. She had already complained of some interference by Fr. Andreotti in the government of the house, but the Mother, on whom the Servant of God depended in everything, had always been informed. These were matters that should not have gone beyond the family of Saint Anne, and in any case were not such as to provoke so severe a measure from the Curia.

During the absence of the Archbishop, who was detained in Rome, the Vicar General had forbidden Fr. Andreotti to concern himself with the house in Via Faenza, as Monsignor Ciaranfi writes: “the said Father received the order with apparent nonchalance, though not without some insistence on the need to give the sisters some help with the schools.”257

Sister Anna del Salvatore was informed of this ban by the Vicar for religious himself and was grieved and dismayed. She in turn wrote to the Mother:

“How much pain I felt and still feel I cannot explain here! Ah, dear Mother, how many things one has to go through! What can this mean?”258

Among the many sorrows the Servant of God suffered, not the least were those caused by the health of some sisters, especially Anna Petronilla, whose condition brought her to the brink of death, so that the doctor no longer knew what to do for her; “indeed he has ordered the Holy Sacraments for her, because he fears she may go without realizing it.” Another sister, Anna Giuseppina, was however recovering.259

Blessed Rosa’s motherly watchfulness extended over the Florence house, distant as it was, and the Servant of God always kept her informed in detail about everything. Sometimes Sister Anna del Salvatore had to correct information that had reached the Foundress by other channels, or urged her to write to the chaplain to satisfy him and stop him complaining about her silence.

Some passages of a letter to Blessed Rosa show with what spirit and good will Sister Anna del Salvatore submitted to the Mother and described the situation of the Florence house.

“As for having a drink out in the city,” she writes on 2 April, “it is true that Sister Anna Narcisa was very thirsty and asked for a little water, and was brought watered wine; so she herself told me. As for the girl [who was asking to be admitted as a postulant], I will do as you say. Dear Mother, I beg you for charity’s sake, if you can, to write just one line to the Chaplain, because every day he keeps saying: does the Mother know that I was the one asked to accept? And why doesn’t she write to me? I tell him: she is so very busy that she really can’t; and he says: perhaps she doesn’t care to? Forgive me, dear Mother, for telling you this, but what can I do, here they are so attached to praise, that is, to courtesies, that one really doesn’t know how to behave. If you like, you can write him just a few lines, that’s enough.”

And again:

“For charity’s sake, if you can, please write a little note to the Chaplain; for now I have nothing else to say.”260

The Mother’s close watch over the Servant of God’s work was not for her a painful, constant exercise of obedience and humility; on the contrary, it gave her the greatest peace of mind when she had to make certain decisions, especially those that might displease someone.

In the case described in April 1878, a priest kept insisting that a young woman who had previously been with the Sisters of Charity be accepted. The priest had come several times to recommend her,

“and I,” writes Sister Anna del Salvatore, “to get rid of him, told him I absolutely cannot, and that he should write to you, and that if the Mother accepts her I am happy. But I warn you that if this girl had been good, the Sisters would not have sent her away, especially as she is an orphan […]. I had to give him [the priest] your address because he kept pestering; perhaps he won’t write to you, but if he does, please don’t accept her.”261

Not the least of the Servant of God’s worries was the shortage, and sometimes total lack, of money, not for herself, as she loved poverty and was used to sacrifice, nor because she despaired of Providence, which never failed the Florence house during her government, but because she could not then support the other works of the Daughters of Saint Anne, for which Mother Gattorno asked, through Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, that money be sent.

“A few lines so as not to tire you,” she wrote to Mother Rosa on 7 April, “and to tell you that yesterday, Saturday, the Sister arrived with the two postulants; she gave me Sister Anna Benedetta’s letter, then told me by word of mouth that I was to give her some money; I would willingly have done so, dear Mother, but I had none, so I could only give them nineteen francs for the journey, as they had nothing. So I could not send the postulant, because the 150 francs she had as a dowry I gave to Fr. Andreotti, and what the Marchioness Covoni brought me I had to use to pay for bread. Then today the one from Cortona came with 150 francs but no money for the journey, because when I asked for it I was told they could not give it, as we should have said so beforehand; so they gave me nothing. Today I sent off both postulants and the two sisters you told me, dear Mother: Sister Anna Cristina and Sister Anna Petronilla.”262

More grieved by the persecution of the Institute than by that of her own person, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote to the Mother:

“My sorrow is as great as can be. Tell me, my little mother, how I should behave with these Florentines. Ah! dear Mother, I no longer know how to deal with these people! Here is yet another sorrow: the doctor has sent me such a stinging letter that it almost drives me out of my mind. Oh, believe me, beloved [Mother], for your sake I am ready to stay here where I am all my life. Yes, my beloved Mother, because of these people I would come to Rome at once. The doctor says he will not come any more because without his order I sent off Sister Anna Giuseppina with bronchitis, fever and chest pain, and that she was a patient who could not possibly be moved, and that I am responsible for this Sister’s health; and I won’t tell you everything because it would cause you too much pain…”

The Mother too was ill in those days, and Sister Anna del Salvatore wished she could do something for her, wished she could visit her and so be more at ease; she asked Jesus that she might suffer those pains instead of the Mother. And at once she corrects herself: “But, my God, what am I saying! Jesus wants you ever holier and so makes you suffer.”263

The accusations against the Daughters of Saint Anne grew more serious; but on what grounds? A Father of the Oratory of San Firenze had reported some rumors he had heard about the immodest behavior of two sisters watching over a sick woman, while the Vicar for religious complained of a girl he saw “leaning out of the window of the House” who “seemed to him a very vain young woman”. He remonstrated with the Superior, who replied that she was a candidate now passing through Florence who would later go to Piacenza.

Because of these facts Monsignor Ciaranfi intended to go to the Daughters of Saint Anne “to give them a little sermon with due delicacy”. He wrote to the Archbishop:

“… Following the death of Cardinal Berardi, perhaps these sisters will have another Most Eminent Protector; let us hope their setup turns out better, that words prove satisfactory, and that the Confessors may have some influence on the good order and morality of the House. If Your Excellency could, or thought fit to, do something for these Sisters in this regard, I believe it could be beneficial. They have a high opinion of the superior general and blindly do whatever She suggests. Fr. Andreotti has withdrawn completely.”264

Canon Ciaranfi had surely understood that the greatest obstacle to his claims and those of the priests who wanted to lay down the law in the house was Sister Anna del Salvatore, despised by them for her simplicity but feared for her loyalty to the “Superior General” (as he called Mother Rosa).

Then, in his correspondence with Monsignor Cecconi, the Vicar for religious, who must have regarded as his own victory the removal of Sister Anna del Salvatore ordered by the Mother when she went to Florence in the last ten days of April, finally reveals his own and the Vicar General’s real aim. In a letter of 27 April, full of details that do not concern the Servant of God’s responsibility but reveal the motives behind the Curia’s behavior towards her, Canon Ciaranfi complains of the Foundress:

“Sister Gattorno came to Florence and Fr. Andreotti went to meet her at the station, but did not go to the Sisters’ House. The said superior has changed the Florence superior and addressed the sisters, telling them that she alone, and no one else, must be informed of any problems that may arise in the Institute, which is purely lay and therefore in no way dependent on ecclesiastical Authority.”

Ciaranfi deplored the frequent visits of Mother Rosa’s relatives to the Florence community, and those of the new superior to San Giovannino, where Fr. Andreotti lived, as well as the “disgraceful” treatment of sick sisters that had supposedly led the doctor Baccani to resign, besides the cases already mentioned, for which, after hearing the Superior, the said Vicar gave the sisters his announced sermon on Easter Monday. Meanwhile, through the Vicar General, he asked the Archbishop to press the new Protector, Cardinal Alessandro Franchi, “begging him, if possible, to take them away from here”, for fear

“that sooner or later some disorder might arise that would embarrass us and cause serious trouble. In any case Monsignor Vicar would like to wash his hands of it and have nothing more to do with it.”265

The situation in Florence could not leave the Foundress indifferent, so that her Memoirs contain some important references to those events, as well as the visions and the explanation Blessed Rosa received supernaturally from Saint Anne about the meaning of a group of rings knotted together, as a warning to prepare to face new and hard trials.

In particular, as regards Sister Anna del Salvatore and the persecution she suffered at that time, these lines from the Memoirs are relevant:

“May 1878: I can say that from the first day until today, the 27th, it has been one continual martyrdom. The troubles in Florence were so tangled, and moreover [I felt] oppressed by something I cannot describe, so that I found it hard to pray: dry and without any comfort.” But a voice encouraged her: “Soon all the persecutions will end.”266

24. - The harsh trial had begun and Sister Anna del Salvatore’s martyrdom continued, though her conscience left her entirely at peace. In these circumstances the resignation she showed in conforming to the Lord’s will and that of her superiors highlighted her candor, her virtues and her innocence.

On 23 April 1878, having left Florence, Sister Anna del Salvatore was already in Osimo, and the next day she would go on to her destination, Appignano.267

Sister Anna Santina Solenghi was sent to replace her in the Florence house, and Mother Rosa did not fail to give her advice and instructions for dealing with the situation. Regarding Sister Anna del Salvatore’s painful case, the Mother told Sister Anna Santina to resist the confessor’s improper pressure, and even suggested the words to use with Canon Ciaranfi should the confessor still insist on interfering in the Institute’s affairs. The words to say to the Vicar were these:

“The confessor would like many things, but we are not enclosed nuns, and I have no intention whatever of doing what he wrongly wants; and anyway leave it to me, I will write to him, that will be better.”268

The days went by and the Mother was ever more worried about the situation: “Oh, what days I am going through because of this house”; “I have no peace night or day”; “I am really on thorns, I can’t tell you what I suffer,” she wrote to Sister Anna Santina on 7 May.

The letter mentions a sister not entirely sound of mind who had defamed Sister Anna del Salvatore and the community by talking about them to the confessor and the Vicar for religious. But the Mother wanted to know who her accomplices were so as to order their transfer. To put a stop to improper interference, Mother Rosa told the new superior that she alone, and no one else, was to deal with the confessor: receive him, attend to him and, as soon as he had finished his ministry, see him out. She also insisted on a clarifying interview with Ciaranfi.269

Faced with the Archbishop’s demand that the sisters withdraw from Florence, Mother Rosa reminded him that Sister Anna del Salvatore had already been replaced and that she had come to Florence to carry this out, in view of the plot hatched by “the sister who left”, whom the confessor had believed.

“But a voice, indeed I heard more than one, said: remove the Superior! And the House will be blown up too,” Mother Rosa’s letter continues, telling how she had gone to the Vicar, who at first agreed with her orders and approved the Servant of God’s replacement, assuring her “that there was nothing in it, and that what had happened [his very words] was childish nonsense”. The slanderer, “placed under strict discipline by the new Superior”, not only complained about it but left the house on her own, went to the confessor, and then with him to Ciaranfi.

The Mother continues:

“The Superior, when told, went to fetch her and took her away, catching the train at once for Piacenza; I do not believe this is an ugly fact that could bring disgrace!!! Your Most Reverend Excellency is too wise not to appreciate what several spiteful and slanderous people are capable of.”

The Mother saw an obvious injustice in the fact that, while in another congregation there had been an enormous scandal without anyone thinking of expelling the sisters from the diocese, the Daughters of Saint Anne were now being treated like this on the basis of unjustifiable resentments and slanders.

The rest of the memorandum, though it does not name Sister Anna del Salvatore, is entirely a recognition of the work done by the Servant of God, a patient sowing whose fruits were now being reaped in spite of everything:

“Listen, Most Reverend Excellency,” writes Mother Rosa, announcing her visit to Florence to inform him better about the matter, “[…]. A house that did and does so much good; the schools were inspected by the Superintendent, who was pleased, so much so that the City Council granted them a salary; the boarders are really doing well and are numerous, and so are the sick; I have very fine letters of thanks, I don’t have them here, but I read them in Florence; there are so many requests that I had to send two more sisters; Providence is very generous […]. I cannot think of something so sad without feeling my heart torn; and if in the past you were pleased with the House, you will be so again; believe me, a great deal of good is being done.”270

Because of slanders as serious as they were groundless, Archbishop Cecconi issued a most unfavorable decision, that they should leave his diocese and withdraw; and on 30 May, from Florence, the Mother appealed for the intervention of the Cardinal Protector, Alessandro Franchi.

In another letter she then begged him to come to Florence to examine the situation and remedy it with his authority.271

It was perhaps still too early for Sister Anna del Salvatore’s full innocence to emerge, or rather for the Florentine Curia to realize the misunderstandings it had fallen into by believing false and malicious rumors. And the Vicar for religious’ mistrust lasted much longer, no longer towards the Servant of God but towards the house itself and those who had taken up its defense and become involved.

After the Mother’s visit to Florence and the departure of the superior she had removed, Canon Ciaranfi had continued to complain to the Archbishop about the Daughters of Saint Anne, dwelling on gossip that did not even concern Sister Anna del Salvatore but discredited the Daughters of Saint Anne, by now disliked by the Vicar, certainly through no fault of theirs. Once again Canon Ciaranfi regretted being unable to intervene to impose his ideas and demands:

“It is certain that this Institute gives cause for concern and fear, and there is no way of supervising it, because the only possible channel is closed, namely that of the confessor, whom their Rules want entirely excluded from the external running of individuals and of the Institute. This is clear from the facts and also from the printed instruction they usually give the confessor, which Your Excellency knows.”

The accusations now reveal the real aim: not content with having had Sister Anna del Salvatore sacrificed, they wanted to drive the sisters out of Florence, appealing for this to the Institute’s new Cardinal Protector.

The Vicar for religious writes further:

“Monsignor Vicar [General] wishes Your Excellency to speak to the aforesaid [Cardinal] about these sisters, asking him if possible to take them away from here, as Monsignor fears that sooner or later some disorder may arise that would embarrass us and cause fresh trouble. In any case Monsignor Vicar would like to wash his hands of it and have nothing more to do with it.”272

On 4 May, from Rome, where he was staying at the Capranica College, the Archbishop, misled by the report he had been given (“also following recent news from Florence”, as he writes), informed Mother Gattorno that the community must urgently be removed, inviting the Foundress

“to take the necessary steps so that, gradually and without publicity, but as soon as possible, the Florence House may be dissolved. Thus the matter will pass unnoticed, as your interest requires.”273

Blessed Rosa, in a letter to Cardinal Franchi, in turn denounced the malicious credulity of the confessor, who, having received the mentally ill sister in his house, as mentioned,

“seized on this fact, saying there is not enough supervision, with a thousand other bits of nonsense added… all invented by him; and in confession he does nothing but speak ill of the Superiors to the Sisters and tries to make them lose their vocation. The worst is that the Vicar for Nuns believes him.”

We already know that the confessor persisted in his aim of turning the house of the Daughters of Saint Anne into an enclosed convent, incompatible with their vocation, and, piqued at not succeeding, spread “certain slanders and truly silly falsehoods, reported to the Curia”, which led to another journey by the Foundress to Florence.274

An authoritative voice, however, was raised in the sisters’ favor, that of Fr. Mauro Ricci, the historian and man of letters whom Leo XIII would call to hold the chair of literature in the higher school he founded and who from 1886 until his death (17 January 1900) would be General of the Piarist Fathers.275 Fr. Ricci, a personal friend of Monsignor Cecconi (with whom he was on familiar terms), advised him not to listen to the rumors going round, and said that because of them he was worried at “not seeing the Archbishop’s name honored as it deserves”.

After this introduction he played down the accusations, while with his Florentine wit he made him see how insubstantial they really were, writing:

“It does not seem to me the right way to go about it, the way certain fussy, touchy people behave, who out of women’s gossip and mere trifles make an argument for telling a religious Institute: Kill yourself. In the end, that is what the demands concerning the Sisters of Saint Anne amount to. Do not believe, I beg you, everything that is being contrived by excellent men who, through inexperience, are fit to understand neither the world nor the cloister.”276

Another defender of the sisters turned out to be Monsignor Giovannini, who, according to Ciaranfi, only three months earlier had accused the Servant of God of lying and put to her the choice: submit or leave Florence;277 now, the truth having been established, he advised Mother Rosa on how to defend herself. Knowing both the Curia and the Daughters of Saint Anne very well, Giovannini knew which strings to pull to avert the expulsion urged by people close to the Archbishop, and at the same time he could vouch for the integrity of Sister Anna del Salvatore and the whole Institute.

He writes to the Foundress:

“Do not be too distressed by the tribulation God has sent you solely in order to establish the Institute more firmly, and not at all to ruin it. For now the matter is proceeding through administrative channels, as was proper, and I do not despair that everything will be settled in this way. I am not surprised that the Archbishop remains firm in his decision; unfortunately that is his habit, which has been the main cause of his ruin in the diocese. He listens only to those three or four suspicious courtiers who play him as they please, leaving all the responsibility to him. Here no one is respected; one has only to disagree to be banished and suspected through the malign influence of the few advisers who scheme in the dark and ruin everything. Prudent men keep silent and simply trust that the truth will make its own way and that Rome will put an end to this mess…”

Meanwhile he recommended

“the greatest prudence, so that nothing happens that could give rise to complaints from the confessor or others. Fr. Zini is convinced, as I am, that this is the best way to proceed in this matter: recollection, silence, caution and courtesy in Florence; energy and firmness in Rome.”278

Although she never again lived permanently in Florence, the Servant of God evidently left behind a firm and undisputed reputation, as Sister Anna Margherita Saggiomo still testified in our own day when she was called to give evidence ex officio at the Palermo Process on 8 April 1999, a hundred and twenty-one years after those events:

“I have always esteemed, and still esteem very highly, Sister Anna del Salvatore, who is for me a daily point of reference, as I have heard many of my other sisters say too.

In Florence, for example, where I was around 1980-86, my sisters showed great esteem for her holiness and considered her always present among them. And when the Florence house, where the Servant of God had been superior, was in danger of being closed, the sisters were deeply convinced that it would not happen, saying: ‘Sister Anna del Salvatore is here at the door and will not allow it.’”279

And so indeed it turned out.

25. - The Servant of God’s new destination was the house at Appignano in the province of Macerata, where Sister Anna del Salvatore had been shortly before as Visitor, as seen in chapter IX.280

The community of the Daughters of Saint Anne had settled there in November 1876, but only at the beginning of the new year had it been able to start its works in schooling and hospital care.

The Marquis Aldobrandino Rangoni Santacroce, who owned an estate in the area, was behind this foundation, which would greatly benefit the rural population.

Rangoni, a former Papal Zouave of Pius IX and a brave fighter on the battlefield and in the defense of Rome, was consistently among the leaders of the Catholic Movement, which aimed among other things to improve living conditions in the countryside and in factories.281

On the advice of Princess Boncompagni Ludovisi, Duchess of Sora, whom we have already seen involved with the houses at Foligno and San Martinello, the Marquis Rangoni had found in the Daughters of Saint Anne exactly what he was looking for for the good of the town. At least four sisters, however, had to go and live there permanently to run the girls’ primary school (which, under ministry regulations, required qualified teachers), the weaving school and the nursing of patients in the small local hospital.

The sisters’ service was paid with a fee of about four lire a day plus free lodging. The offer was accepted, and after the agreement had been ratified in Piacenza with the archpriest of Appignano and the Marquis Rangoni, Sister Anna Eufemia Camporesi, superior and schoolteacher, went to Appignano with three other sisters.

On 2 January 1877 the primary classes began with a fair attendance (35-40 girls), while the workshop was being set up with modern looms like those in use at the Mother House in Piacenza, also obtained by the Foundress. The hospital, which at the time had a single patient, was restored and given regulations. It too soon prospered; but above all Appignano produced some vocations in those years, starting with the first six girls who, right after Mother Rosa’s visit (23 May 1877), left for the postulancy in Piacenza (27 May).

When the Servant of God arrived, that community was already successfully carrying on the welfare works entrusted to it by the municipality, as well as parish work, always with charity, diligence and competence. For eighty years, until the year it closed (1958), the sisters’ house was a vital center for the town.

As it was impossible to continue the journey the same day, the Servant of God had spent the night at the bishop’s residence in Osimo, since it did not seem proper to her to stay at an inn, and she could not travel on to Appignano at night. But she was troubled by scruples, as her instructions had been to go straight to her destination without stopping anywhere. So Sister Anna del Salvatore hastened to inform the Foundress as soon as she reached Osimo:

“For charity’s sake, good Mother… finding myself in this situation I chose to sleep here, because if it had been daytime we would rather have gone on foot, but it was already six o’clock, so I was afraid of doing worse; so tomorrow morning we shall leave early, straight after the Bishop’s Mass.”282

On joining that community Sister Anna del Salvatore found “a house stripped of everything and very little money in the cash box”, few provisions, the clock broken (she had to borrow one from the parish priest) and little discipline, because the previous superior, in poor health, had not been able to carry out her role fully. In this way the Servant of God excused her sisters’ small breaches of discipline.283

The Mother had forbidden her to write to Florence, and Sister Anna del Salvatore asked her how she could forward a certain sum of money that had come into her hands, while also informing her of what was happening in the Appignano house, the money received and the expenses incurred.284

Always thinking of others, as when she asked that the allowance the Florence house paid to a sister’s mother be continued,285 Sister Anna del Salvatore informed the Foundress of certain facts and asked for her decision on them;286 meanwhile the situation was improving, as the provost of Appignano had just bought a house for the sisters,

“and from this week,” Sister Anna del Salvatore had written in her previous letter, “he is putting the builders in, and then we shall be able to go to church without going outside.”287

The Mother’s permission to renew her vows and her invitation to the spiritual exercises in Piacenza were received with joy and gratitude, so much so that the Servant of God, unaware of what was about to happen to her, wrote: “Jesus alone can reward you for all the goodness and charity you show me.” Sister Anna del Salvatore was, however, troubled by the house’s financial situation, burdened, through no fault of hers, with various debts.

A valuable testimony given by Sister Anna Letizia Sordi in her report to Mother Carrega sheds light on the short time the Servant of God spent in Appignano. The episodes recounted, in keeping with what we know of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s mystical gifts and intensity of prayer, also explain the origin of the reputation that surrounded her even in her lifetime, although she kept hiding and concealing extraordinary happenings.

Her fellow sister wrote about this as an eyewitness:

“In 1878, when she was in Piacenza in April, at the Elevation of Holy Mass she heard a voice saying to her: You are going to Appignano and you will see Clementina (that was [my] name in the world). At the beginning of May she was sent by the Superior General to Appignano. She told me this herself. The same year, as the vote for the election of town councillors was to be held in Appignano, the Rev. Provost commended the outcome to her prayers. During the voting Sister Anna del Salvatore said to us in a prophetic tone these exact words: Be happy, it has gone well. After midday what she said proved true.”

And linking two episodes that apparently both occurred in the little town in the Marche at almost the same time, the sister writes:

“The same year, while we were in church for morning prayers, when it was customary to recite the ‘Remember, O Our Lady’, on reaching the words ‘No, we cannot, etc.’, she vanished from the sisters’ sight. One of them ran at once to catch up with her. She was searched for at length but was not found until several hours later.

Another time, in 1878, in the public church of Appignano, shortly after Holy Communion she left her pew saying: Let’s go. The sister next to her, Sister Anna Pacifica, however fast she ran after her, could not catch up. She seemed to have wings on the stairs… Reaching the nearest room, which belonged to the infirmarian sister, she locked herself in, all in a flash, and threw herself on her knees, her eyes full of tears turned and fixed on heaven, her arms outstretched in the form of a cross, speaking a language we did not understand. We could see this through the keyhole, because the key was turned in such a way that we could see everything. We knocked hard at the door and called her for a long time; she gave no sign of hearing us. After a while she came out and seemed embarrassed in front of us, saying she had done one of her usual things, and calling herself mad, a mole, out of her mind.”288

Her stay in Appignano had left a sweet memory in Sister Anna del Salvatore’s heart, and she looked back with moving nostalgia to the busy calm of that town in the Marche and the harmony with her sisters and the people during difficult days such as those she spent among the “Penitents” in Rome.

On 14 November 1878 she wrote to Sister Anna Letizia Sordi, who had remained in Appignano:

“Beloved sister, my Letizia, if I may still call you so… Tell me, my dear, how are you? Oh, how often you come to my mind… Mine for ever, I would love a letter from you, because I fear you are not well; poor thing, who knows how much you suffer; I seem to see you, yes, I seem to hear you with that nasty cough… Oh dearest, how great is my sorrow!”

Remembering one by one the sisters still in that house, she asks for news of them: Anna Corinna, Anna Beniamina, Anna Pacifica (“is she still always sighing?”), Anna Natalina (“what is she doing with her looms?”), and adds: “Have they forgotten their poor sister, Sister Anna del Salvatore? Yes, they have certainly forgotten, haven’t they? I haven’t, I really haven’t; and Sister Anna Letizia, she doesn’t forget poor me, does she?”

She also remembered the benefactresses and the Provost, and “the great kindness” one of them, Signora Lui, had shown her when she accompanied her to Loreto in stormy weather.

In all this we see the spirit and sensitivity of the Servant of God, her goodness and humility, virtues that constantly surface in the warm-hearted spontaneity of her character.289

If in the letter of 28 July the Servant of God had been saddened at being unable to bring money to the Mother, a few days later she was struck by a far deeper sorrow on receiving the command to attend the exercises “under obedience” (which she would joyfully have done anyway). Regarding this formal obligation almost as a punishment for having asked the Provost of Appignano, rather than the Mother, which Superior (of the nearest house) should be her companion on the journey to Piacenza, the Servant of God had no idea that in reality the order carried consequences.

So, with surprise and sorrow, but with her usual humility and trust, her usual affection for the Mother, and also for reasons of justice, she hastened to write to the Foundress:

“Dear beloved Mother. Ah, what sorrow has just come to me, so unexpectedly! How could it ever be that I would not want to obey, when I am so happy to be able to see you? And how could I go on living if even for a single moment such a thought had crossed my mind? My God!… after so much joy when I heard I was to come and make the holy Exercises, I now have to feel this sharp pain that my dear Mother should have to oblige me under obedience.”290

The nightmare of the Florence affair, which not even her removal had helped to resolve, must certainly have returned to her mind; and so delicate and humble was her conscience that Sister Anna del Salvatore, while reproaching herself for non-existent faults, showed truly exemplary resignation, as great as the pain she felt, and silently faced the harsh trial.

26. - In Piacenza, where she had promptly gone in obedience to the formal command, Sister Anna del Salvatore faced the most painful trial of her life, compared with which her past tribulations must have seemed very light. Now it seemed that, rather than moving, as she had, from running an important city house to running a small community in a minor town, the Servant of God was actually to be expelled from the Institute as unworthy, no longer to work with Mother Rosa, no longer to wear the habit, no longer to be a Daughter of Saint Anne.

When the Mother informed the superiors of the situation in Florence, which had become so serious that the Archbishop had called for the sisters’ withdrawal, some sisters, holding the Servant of God responsible for it all, asked for her dismissal, while others hastened to ask forgiveness for the mistakes she was supposed to have made.

As things stood, almost all the sisters gathered for the spiritual exercises considered her guilty in principle, though, as mentioned, some would lighten the penalty by excusing those supposed faults as the result of inexperience.291

Some testimonies about the events of that summer of 1878 and Sister Anna del Salvatore’s behavior were written thirty-five years later, with order and precision despite the time elapsed, by Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi and Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, and later included in the Informative Process. The former had known the Servant of God’s virtues well since her novitiate in Piacenza and had always been edified by “her humble and recollected bearing, her manner full of gentleness and charity towards all and her exact observance of her religious duties”.

“And from then on,” she states, “I regarded her as a truly beautiful soul dear to the Lord.” Having said that this opinion grew as they nursed the sick together, Sister Anna Elisabetta, returning to the very sad days of the trial, continues:

“We traveled together from Loreto to Piacenza; I was coming from Acquaviva and she from a house near Loreto; we met there and got into the same compartment. In this circumstance, painful for her too, since by all accounts she had been unjustly accused, or rather slandered, I was able to admire her great virtue and humility. When we met she said to me: ‘This morning I went to confession and received Holy Communion in the Holy House; whatever happens, I am at peace and entirely abandoned to my Lord.’ Did she perhaps know what was being said against her? I don’t know!… During the journey, it was August and very hot, and everyone felt the need to refresh themselves from time to time; she did not take even a drop of water, and remained fasting until late the next day, and received Holy Communion and heard Holy Mass with me in the Capuchin Fathers’ church, as it had already been celebrated in the Mother House by the late hour we arrived.”

Sister Anna Elisabetta also mentions the recollection and devotion with which the Servant of God made the exercises, at the end of which word spread again of serious accusations against her and of the humiliation awaiting her.292

Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, her former companion in Florence, left a further testimony dated 5 March 1913, confirming that this was “the pure and holy truth”.

“I am a witness of a humiliation she underwent in the Mother House in Piacenza,” she writes in the Recollections to be kept concerning Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi. “She was charged with a serious fault, unknown to me; not seeing her with us as usual, I went to look for her and found her alone in the dormitory, holding a bundle of letters. I asked her: ‘What are you doing here? What are those papers in your hand?’ She answered: ‘They are letters from the Mother [General].’ ‘Well,’ I added, ‘what are you doing with these letters?’ Very gently, but deeply grieved, she said: ‘I have heard that today they will take my Holy Veil from me, and I will hand these letters to the Mother; I will not resist at all, I will do as Isaac did, who sacrificed his life. I will lay my head on the Mother’s knees, as Isaac lay on the bundle of wood; let her do as she wishes, I will not resist at all; but if I have to leave the Institute, I will try in my littleness to do as much good as I can for the Institute, and if need be I will even go begging to help it.’ I admired great virtue in her: not a word in her own defense, no complaint, but great humility and resignation.”293

The “Recollections” of Sister Anna Camilla Valentini, also written in 1913 when she was Assistant General, document the same events with further details worth reporting:

“I was summoned [from Borgo San Donnino, where I was superior], but could not go until the last day, that is, the closing day [of the spiritual exercises in the Mother House]. On arriving in Piacenza many Superiors told me that on that day Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi was to be stripped of the habit and sent away from the Institute. Without asking the reason for such a decision, I asked where Sister Anna del Salvatore was: ‘In church,’ I was told; and indeed she was there, wholly absorbed in prayer, calm and serene. I went down to the garden, where there were sisters, asked a few questions to find out something, and met Sister Anna Celsa Speranza, now Secretary General. I asked her if she knew the reason for what was to happen, and she said no. A certain Sister Anna Palmira Grillotti joined us, saying: ‘Come along too, let us all go together to ask the Mother’s forgiveness for Sister Anna del Salvatore.’”294

Together with those other sisters, Anna Elisabetta Veronesi went to ask the Mother “for the favor that such a decision not be taken; we did so and obtained everything”.295

Sister Anna Camilla added:

“Several superiors went to the chapel to tell her that the Mother had forgiven her, and she joyfully thanked first the Lord and then the Mother and all of us.”296

That Sister Anna del Salvatore had nothing to be forgiven had already been recognized, even before Sister Anna Camilla Valentini brought it out in her “sworn” testimony at the Roman Process of the Foundress:

“[…] To our words the Servant of God, now Blessed Rosa, replied: ‘But forgiveness for what? Sister A. del Salvatore is not at fault at all, and I am ready to embrace her.’”297

Her resignation in the face of the threat of such an injustice had been exemplary, and Sister Anna Elisabetta had noted Sister Anna del Salvatore’s expression as

“a little sad, but with a calm, resigned sadness, ready for anything, yet always loving and praying for the dear Institute; not one word of excuse or defense passed her lips; on the contrary, she said to me: ‘Ah! if the Lord did not keep his most holy Hands on my head, I could do this and worse’; and, wholly abandoned in the Lord’s hands, she entrusted her defense to him, who, if he puts his beloved to hard trials, never fails afterwards to make their innocence and holiness shine more brightly; and so he did with this Servant of his.”

Sister Anna Elisabetta also recalls that in those days the Servant of God had lost her Crucifix and she wanted to give her another one she had just received as a gift. But Sister Anna del Salvatore would not accept it without first getting the Mother’s permission, so great was “the delicacy of her conscience”.298

All this is confirmed in particular by the testimony of Sister Anna Camilla Valentini quoted above.

Her rehabilitation was not yet complete and had not yet been made known, presumably for fear that this “acquittal for not having committed the act” might be interpreted in Florence as a condemnation of the Curia’s schemes against the Institute, the Foundress and the Servant of God, her faithful and devoted agent. Consequently, since no final word had yet been said on the survival of the house, some dangerous turn in the affair could be feared, just when the Curia’s hostility was easing.299

So the Servant of God, instead of returning to Florence fully vindicated, or to Appignano, where the sisters so eagerly awaited and loved her (so much so that, according to Sister Anna Pacifica, her failure to return was “a real wound to the heart”300), humbly accepted, as an ordinary sister, an assignment to Ferrara. In that environment, which soon proved hostile to her, the Servant of God stayed only a few months, while in Florence the situation was settling down with the revocation of the Archbishop’s measure.

The Ferrara house had been founded with the help of Countess Maria Anna Trotti, who thereby fulfilled a vow made to Saint Anne while a lawsuit (over her husband’s inheritance) was pending, later settled in her favor.

Mother Rosa cared about this foundation too, and Countess Trotti confided in her and received advice and comfort from her. Mother Gattorno went to Ferrara to visit the benefactress and see the house intended for the Institute’s works, and always supported the venture, even when the benefactress’s help ceased, just when the schools were flourishing with about a hundred pupils and the sisters’ nursing was in demand everywhere.301

For the Servant of God, as mentioned, that stay brought further sorrows, always borne with faith and with charity towards those who persecuted her. People there were prejudiced against her, and some felt it their duty to correct and almost punish her. It must have been a very painful stay indeed if for a moment Sister Anna del Salvatore was assailed by the temptation to go home, where her relatives, still unaware of what had happened, would have welcomed her back, leaving her free in her religious and charitable practices and even ready to fit out a chapel where she could withdraw and carry on the usual practices of religious life.302 Sister Anna del Salvatore could have helped serve the parish and the faithful, and her uncle Don Luigi Mussi, who had always admired her virtues, would have offered her a wide field of apostolate. It was said that at that juncture her Guardian Angel appeared to the Servant of God during the journey to Ferrara and “told her to obey and continue her journey”.303

It should be noted, however, that all this is reported by people who had heard of it from others, and her wavering is not very convincing, since Sister Anna del Salvatore had borne far greater difficulties without feeling inclined to exchange suffering for a calmer, more peaceful life of contemplation and activity with her uncle.

Indeed, despite these sad events, the Servant of God had remained “good, humble and charitable with everyone”,304 entrusting her cause to the Lord, certain that he would make the truth, threatened by mistrust and slander, shine out, as indeed happened.305
